utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Niemann, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honours, I will present argument additional to our written submissions on the first part of our response referred to in part II as The establishment of the Tribunal is a legitimate exercise of the Security Council powers under Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter. This section of the Prosecution response addresses in part the Defence arguments contained in paragraphs 1 through to 7 of the Defence motion. Mr. Fenrick will deal with part III of the Defence response entitled the Applicability of Subject Matter Jurisdiction. This section of the Prosecution submission addresses in part paragraphs 8 through to 12 of the Defence argument of the motion. Any submissions I will now make are supplemental to and will not purport to traverse our written statement, except that it is necessary for the purposes of addressing any questions that your Honours may raise or in dealing with matters that were raised by the Defence yesterday. Your Honour, at the outset there is one issue that was raised by Mr. Wladimiroff yesterday that I would like to address now. That relates to the question of review of the decision of the Security Council. The Defence seek to rely on a reference to the right to be tried by a court established by law to be found in Article 14 of the International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights as support for the proposition that this Tribunal may review the decisions of the Security Council. In my submission, this confuses the issue. The Tribunal must ensure that the accused is given a fair trial. If the Security Council did something when creating the Tribunal which prevented the Tribunal from giving the accused a fair trial, the issue, in my submission, is not to be resolved by doing something which the International Court of Justice itself finds that it cannot do, namely, to review the decisions of the Security Council, but by declining to extend the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to try the case until that impediment to a fair trial is removed. So, in my submission, the appropriate course is to stay the proceedings if that eventuality arose.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Neimann, stay the proceedings and do what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission, if the accused was to point to something which demonstrated that because of an irregularity in the creation of the Tribunal he cannot receive a fair trial, my submission is one does not go into review of that decision as such; one simply says that the trial cannot be fair and, therefore, it is not appropriate to extend the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to allow the trial to take place.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If we say that the trial is not fair because of one of the impediments that the Defence raised, then we would be reviewing those very alleged impediments. We would be thus reviewing the decision of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In a sense, that is true, your Honour, but not quite so. The position is, your Honour, that it needs to be more than simply saying, we do not think it is something that comes within the ambit of Article 41 of the United Nations Charter, or that this is not really a situation where there is a threat to international peace and security under Article 39. It is not that. It is really pointing to something which is arbitrary, capricious. There was speak yesterday of naming accused with white hair, a bill of attainder. All those matters may well prevent this Tribunal delivering a fair trial. If that happened, the effect is probably the same. The effect is: "Well, we cannot hear this case, because that is our primary responsibility. So we decline to extend jurisdiction until that impediment is removed". It may mean that there are no trials in that circumstance. But it is not a case of embarking upon an examination of the course adopted by the Security Council in first instance, and saying: "This is a right which is derived from", for example, "Article 14 of the Covenant". It does not arise in that circumstance, in our submission. It arises because the Defence raise an issue such as the Security Council has declared that all people with white hair are to be tried for war crimes. When confronted with that issue that would be, in my submission, the appropriate response for this Tribunal...

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then are you saying that the Tribunal does have at least a limited right of review in so far as we can determine whether or not the decision of the Security Council was arbitrary?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In a very limited extent, your Honours would probably go into that issue because your Honours must be satisfied that you can deliver a fair trial, that these proceedings are fair. So, on any matter that is raised by the Defence it is necessary to examine them to see that is the case, that a fair trial can be delivered. It is a question of in what depth one goes and the issue raised. So, if something is raised which is capricious, which is arbitrary, which stands in the face of a fair trial, then one examines in greater depth. If, however, the only issue is: "We do not think that Article 41 should be interpreted as broadly as the Security Council has done so", and that when one looks at the action taken by the Security Council everything else seems to be regular, one then does not say: "Well, we will go behind that and make a decision on the breadth of Article 41 and what the Security Council can do", in my submission. So it is a prime facie examination dealt with on the issues raised by the Defence. If you are satisfied that the Security Council did everything appropriately, there is nothing to point to arbitrariness, there is nothing to point to capriciousness, then that is the end of the examination, in our submission. It is our submission that one proceeds almost on the basis there is a presumption of regularity in what has happened. So one can rest on the decision so long as those parameters that are set out in the Charter seemed to have been complied with, and you are satisfied that that is so, but you do not need to go any further, in our submission Your Honour, the Defence also raised an argument in relation to special courts and ad hoc courts, and they make mention of the Human Rights Committee established under Article 28 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. In our submission, that reference does not specifically prohibit the creation of special courts as such. What it really does is it says if special courts are created, then there must be an assurance that all full judicial guarantees are provided which, in our submission, is the case with this Tribunal because of the guarantees that are provided for the defendant. Just dealing with another issue that was raised by the Defence yesterday in relation to the evocando test. In our submission, that may have application in some jurisdictions -- we do not deny that -- but we would say that certainly it is not universal and such a principle, if it were to apply, would impact upon and affect the traditional extradition operations of states, because if it was to apply universally then, presumably, that would be a bar to extradition in most instances, and because of that and because of the fact that extradition is commonly applied by states, we say that it cannot be an international principle, a universal principle as such.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But even we do not have to deal with that; do we not have a different situation here? Do not we have Article 24 of the Charter that would require states or, at least, an argument can be made that it would require states to comply with decisions of the Security Council including the decision it makes under Article 39?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is in addition to that. Your Honour, there are a couple of citations that we would wish to deal which, we may suggest, are not strictly accurate that the Defence made yesterday that we will deal with when we look at the transcript more closely of the latter part of yesterday. It is not significant matters, but there are some arguments. I will come back to that when I have had an opportunity to look at the transcript. Dealing with paragraph 1.1 of the Defence Motion, the Defence say that any jurisdiction exercised by the International Tribunal can only be established by taking into account state sovereignty. In the context of the Defence submission, we assume that this is more to do with the conferral of jurisdiction upon the Tribunal by the Security Council rather than the exercise of that jurisdiction once conferred. In relation to this, we make two points. Firstly, if there is such an obligation under international law, we are not aware of its application in the context of the establishment of this Tribunal. Secondly, the whole process of establishing a United Nations in the first place, and especially conferring of specific powers on one of its organs or any number of its organs, but, in particular, the Security Council, necessitates in part a surrender of sovereignty by individual states, plus the fact that there is an international interest by a community of nations means that the individual sovereignty concerns of a particular state are subordinate to the greater international community interest. Indeed, a reading preamble to the United Nations Charter illustrates this point when it speaks of the common interests of nations. Further, Article 24 of the UN Charter gives the Security Council primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. Then in the carrying out of this duty, the Security Council acts on behalf of individual states. Article 25 provides that members agree to accept and carry out the decisions of the Security Council in accordance with the Charter. To the extent that state sovereignty is protected in the context of the United Nations, such protection does not extend to the creation of this Tribunal because sub-article 7 of Article 2 specifically provides that the interests of states, domestic jurisdiction, in other words, its sovereignty, shall not prejudice the application of enforcement measures under Chapter VII of the UN Charter. In our submission, the creation of this Tribunal is such a measure. A further illustration of the limitation on state sovereignty can be found in sub-Article 1 of Article 12 of the Charter which expressly provides that while the Security Council is exercising its functions, the General Assembly shall not make any recommendations with regard to that situation unless the Security Council so requests. In our submission, this limitation on the General Assembly which represents the interests of individual states is a further inroad, as it were, on to the question of state sovereignty. In paragraph 1.1 of the Defence argument, they rely on specific United Nations documents in support of their argument that the creation of the Tribunal should have been based on a treaty. But each document referred to when read in its entirety does not, in reality, support the argument because, for a variety of reasons, they conclude in support of the establishment of the Tribunal by action of the Security Council. Further, in paragraph 1.1 the Defence argue that states should be given an opportunity to make known their approval or disapproval for the establishment of an ad hoc Tribunal. However, a significant number of states did participate in this process. In the Security Council, all 15 member-states unanimously voted in favour of the establishment of a Tribunal and 30 states participated in the overall process of establishment of the Tribunal. After all, the Nuremberg Statute itself only had the participation of four states and the United Nations Charter itself initially only had participation of 50 states. Besides, surely, even if a state does raise an objection to the creation of a body such as the Tribunal, such individual opposition cannot mean that the validity of the Statute of the tribunal is then brought into question. Minority opposition by states to a decision of the Security Council is not relevant to the question of the validity of an action by the Security Council under Chapter VII.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, the Defence would say that is not much of a participation, the fact that they may have spoken, some states, in favour of the establishment of the Tribunal. They say that it is the body that should have, it was not preferable, but it is the body that should have established the Tribunal, not the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The General Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, General Assembly. What they say is: "Well, that is fine, but some states may have expressed approval, other states expressed disapproval. In order to get the full input from the member-states the way that the Tribunal should be established, and must be established, is by the General Assembly".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that argument, your Honour, but the point we are making in our submissions is that when one considers other very significant charters which have been established in history, we see that, for example, Nuremberg had the participation, as I say, of the four states and the United Nations Charter itself had 50 and in this case we had the 15 Security Council members and 30. So even though the participation level is not universal, it is, in our submission, significant. In any event, there is a mechanism by which states could participate. They could make submissions to the Secretary General and a number of states were invited to and did so. So it is not as though it was something that was just rushed through the Security Council with a majority support without veto; it did go through a process where participation occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I gather the only way that the General Assembly could have established the Tribunal would have been through amending the Charter, from listening to the Defence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is our argument, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If the General Assembly had begun that process, whatever that process might have been before the Security Council determined that there was a threat of peace, would that have prevented the Security Council from going forward?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would not have thought so, your Honour. The fact that there is an ongoing process is one thing; the fact that the Security Council deems it necessary to take emergency measures under Article 42 is another. I think one does not preclude the other.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because the General Assembly or, at least, the International Law Commission, I gather, has been considering for 40 years, I think Mr. Wladimiroff said yesterday, the establishment of a permanent International Criminal Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that is something, at least, that they have been thinking about and taking some action on, I guess, but once the Security Council then enters this area, that they have primary power over under Article 39, you would say, then they are permitted to proceed and, in a sense, their action supersedes the General Assembly's discussions about the establishment of a Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission, that is the position. Contrary to the Defence Motion at paragraph 1.1, the treaty approach was not the proper approach because, clearly, the establishment of the Tribunal by the Security Council exercising Chapter VII powers, as opposed to the establishment by a treaty, was the preferred course, especially having regard to the urgency attached to the matter by the Security Council. In paragraph 1.2, the Defence seem to confuse what the International Law Commission is doing with what the Security Council did when it created the Tribunal, and this touches upon the point just raised by your Honour. The international law Commission's approach of establishing a permanent criminal tribunal by treaty in no way derogates, in our submission, from the establishment of an ad hoc Tribunal by the Security Council. The two methods of creating Tribunals can comfortably sit side by side without being in conflict of each other. Besides, the draft Statute of the permanent Tribunal contemplates that the Security Council itself may take action under Chapter VII, notwithstanding the opposition of particular states, in order to refer matters to it. The Defence go on to assert in paragraph 1.3 that the establishment of an ad hoc tribunal undermines the initiative of establishing a permanent tribunal. There are, I think, two responses to this proposition. Firstly, the appropriate and fundamental issue for consideration at the end of the day is to determine whether a fair trial can be assured. There is absolutely nothing to say that a permanent tribunal would be better placed to dispense justice than an ad hoc tribunal, provided the guarantees of a fair trial are incorporated in the ad hoc tribunal. Secondly, it is difficult to understand why or how an ad hoc tribunal undermines the creation of a permanent tribunal as there must, surely, be an equally valid opposite argument to the effect that the successful creation and operation of an ad hoc tribunal enhances the prospect of achieving a permanent tribunal but, in any event, we ask: Why is this issue relevant to this debate? In paragraph 2.1, the Defence argument, they speak in terms of Security Council overlooking the General Assembly. There is no evidence to support the inference by the Defence that the General Assembly has somehow been overlooked by the Security Council when taking its action. Once the Security Council took the action, the General Assembly would not have interfered in any event as the taking of the action by the Security Council restricts the activities of the General Assembly. Besides, we have not been able to find any evidence to support the suggestion that the General Assembly was not in favour of action taken by the Security Council in establishing this Tribunal. Accordingly, if one accepts, firstly, that serious violations of international humanitarian law have been committed in the territory of former Yugoslavia, secondly, that such violations constitute a threat to international peace and security within the meaning of Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, thirdly, that the establishment of the Tribunal is an appropriate measure to maintain or restore international peace and security, then the General Assembly is by definition excluded under the United Nations Charter as this is a matter exclusively within the province of the Security Council. So, contrary to what the Defence assert in paragraph 2.4, the General Assembly would not have the competence to establish the Tribunal in these circumstances in any event. I suggest that because yesterday Mr. Wladimiroff seemed to say that the most appropriate course -- I think he referred to it as the "Royal Road" -- was the amendment to the Charter itself. Just while I am at this point, your Honour, it is these tests that, I submit, are appropriate for consideration in determining the issue of whether this Tribunal has been appropriately and properly established according to law, to look at these questions and to determine them on these bases without necessity of going further or beyond that. So, the same test, in my submission, applies because that is the test that gives the Security Council the power, in our submission, to create the Tribunal. Once satisfied that those measures have been complied with in accordance with that test, then that is the end of the examination of the matter, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Should we review then those predicate decisions by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In our submission, it is appropriate to do so in the context of determining whether in any matter raised by the Defence could interfere with the ability to provide for a fair trial. In our submission, none of those matters go into that question and you need not go beyond it. But it seems to me, your Honour, that the necessity to provide for a fair trial is all pervasive in a criminal court. There is some legitimacy, in our submission, for the argument that an International Court of Justice is not confronted with the same issues that confront a criminal court. So, it is, in our submission, necessary in order to satisfy yourselves that a fair trial can be rendered to, at least, look prime facie at these issues. In a context of a state, for example, in the creation of a court there, if one was determining, is it in accordance with law, the examination need go no further, perhaps, than saying, was it an Act of the Parliament of the state that created the court? If one is satisfied that that is the case, then that, in our submission, is the end of the matter. It is only if something can be pointed to which is capricious, which is arbitrary, that that would raise a need for a greater examination; not so that you would end or conclude by saying the Security Council (a) does not have the power to create the body it created or (b) that whatever it did was illegal or invalid, not for that purpose, but in order to satisfy yourselves that that problem, that impediment, that irregularity, is not something that impedes the right to a fair trial. Once you have satisfied yourselves of that, that is as far as you have to go, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you this? Where do you find this overriding requirement that whatever the Security Council does, it should be such as to ensure a Tribunal which can give a fair trial? Because you put that as a test that we should apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is part of international law, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is part of international law that a fair trial of accused persons will be rendered. We would submit that the Security Council would not or should not take steps or measures which fly in the face of that. If they did it, then that may not necessarily mean that the Tribunal does not operate; what it means is that the Tribunal must examine that and make a determination of whether or not that irregularity impacts upon the ability to provide for a fair trial. So it would, in our submission, be appropriate for your Honours to conclude, if the issue is raised -- and I stress that it has not been raised -- for your Honours to say: "There is an irregularity here; the Security Council should have done this or should have done something else. That has been raised by the Defence and pointed to, but that does not impact upon us. That does not prevent us from providing for a fair trial. We can do that notwithstanding this irregularity". In our submission, the matter should then proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What about the other criterion suggested, namely, established by law; do we have to satisfy ourselves that what the Security Council did is "law"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, in the sense of in the context of whether or not a fair trial can be provided for, and only in that context. So, the resolution of that is a prime facie examination of it. It is not something that is done completely without -- there are, if I can come at it another way, limitations on what the Security Council can do. I am not in a position to list all of them, but we would argue that if the Security Council did proceed by way of bill of attainder, for example, that may well be an issue that would trouble this Tribunal. It may not trouble it to the point where it declares that the act was invalid, but it may trouble it in the provision of the jurisdiction for the purposes of that trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 20 Article 20, Part 1 of the Statute provides that the Trial Chambers shall ensure that a trial is fair and expeditious etc. etc., but that is in the Statute and it says that the Trial chamber shall ensure that a trial is fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I presume that you would admit, at least, that the Defence has raised that issue? I am not sure, you said something earlier and I was not clear whether you were saying that they had raised the issue or not, but it seems to me what they are saying is, because of the way that the Security Council created the Tribunal, that there really was not a threat to peace and that it does not fit within the measures of Article 41, and the whole political nature of it, which I am sure you will respond to. It is saying that the accused cannot get a fair trial. So, perhaps, our jurisdictional basis, Article 22 -- is that what I just read?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Article 20, sub-article 1.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 20, part 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to that question is this, it is not raised in the context of a conferral upon this Tribunal of the jurisdiction to examine, if I call it "jurisdiction", though I do not really regard it as jurisdiction in the traditional sense, but it does not confer upon this Tribunal the loosely phrased jurisdictional terms to examine the actions of the Security Council which is a principal organ of the United Nations and which the International Court of Justice itself says it cannot do. That has not been conferred, in our submission. So, it is not appropriate for this Tribunal then to embark upon an examination of what the Security Council did in the creation of a Tribunal, except if it can be shown by something raised by the Defence that whatever they did would impact upon the ability to render a fair trial. In our submission, that has never been raised. There is nothing the Defence have ever pointed to to suggest that. They simply say that it is their right because they are entitled to have an examination of whether or not the Tribunal was created by law. In our submission, in dealing with the Defence motion on this, one merely examines, was it created by law. One does it prima facie. It was done under the International Charter; it was done pursuant to Chapter VII; it fits within those parameters. That is the end of the examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Defence is not saying that there is anything in the Statute that was drafted by a Secretary General that somehow denies the accused a fair trial. That seems to be what you are saying. They are not pointing to anything that specifically denies him a fair trial. It seems to me that, as I understand it, what you are saying is they have to say there is something about this Tribunal, what it provides, that denies the accused a right to a fair trial. They are not saying that. They are saying that the very establishment denies the accused a right to a fair trial because the actions of the Secretary General were arbitrary, because they were political, not well-founded, not consistent, and that those very actions were arbitrary, and that then the creation of the Tribunal creates an institution that cannot by its very nature give an accused a fair trial. So they are not pointing to any impediments in the Statute, they are pointing to the very establishment -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My use of the term "arbitrary" may be a problem -- I mean "arbitrary" in a capricious sense. If the Statute was: "Everyone shall be prosecuted whose name starts with A" would be arbitrary and capricious; the two must go together. I mean, there is an element of arbitrariness in everything, in any political decision that is made, because any decision that is made by a body, such as the Security Council, or a parliament of a state, or legislature, is done on the basis of the issues that arise before it as it goes along. There is always an argument can be raised: "Well, this was arbitrary because it did not do it here and it did not do it there", but that is not the point. The point is when you couple an arbitrary decision with a capricious decision, and we submit that nothing has been pointed to to say that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying then that we may review to determine whether what the Security Council provided is arbitrary and capricious and, thus, denies the accused a right to a fair trial? Or are you saying that we may determine whether its very establishment of the Tribunal was based on arbitrary and capricious considerations?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not exactly saying either of those things, your Honour. What I am saying is this, that the accused must raise before you a factor which he points to and says: "That prevents me from having a fair trial".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: A factor where, a factor within the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A factor anywhere, but in the context of this debate, in the creation of a Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In the creation of a Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that is what he does. He purports to call for an examination of the process of creation and the powers of the Security Council in the context of what he says is entitled to be tried by a tribunal established by law.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that something that we can look at, to determine whether it is arbitrary and capricious?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The answer to that is no, not if you are satisfied that the process that was applied -- not unless it is raised by them. Firstly, it has not been raised, but if it were raised, only to the extent that that may impact upon a fair trial. So even if you did find that it was arbitrary and capricious, but yet you were still able to provide for a fair trial, then that would be the course that you should follow, provide for a fair trial, because that is the requirement of the Statute. The Statute is limited in its jurisdiction. The Tribunal does not have a wide ranging jurisdiction that covers all matters. I do not need to take your Honours to the point to show that. So the issue that you really must always deal with (and which gives a much greater breadth to the area of examination than which ordinarily would be available to you) is the issue of a fair trial. So, if somebody can legitimately raise the question which points to an impact upon that ability to provide for that, then that opens the doors to an examination wider than what would ordinarily be available.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has, in your opinion, the Defence pointed to such things?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is because he has just focused on the establishment of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Exactly and said: "It is arbitrary; they have not done it in any other cases". In my submission, that does not come anywhere near it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That just goes to the merits of what he has alleged, but has he alleged the type of actions which, if we agreed with, would be arbitrary and capricious?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What are the types of things that he could state (without presenting an argument for the Defence) that would be the kind of issue that we could look at to determine whether or not it impacted the right to a fair trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That the Statute -- I will just raise a few -- says that the accused has no right of appearance, that the hearings are to take place in camera, and that the accused is not entitled to be present nor to be represented, may be an issue, if it specifically spelt that out; if it said: "People shall be presumed guilty until they prove their innocence" in a sense that they are guilty and it is for them, given an opportunity, to dispel that. I could go on, but they are the sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then I do understand. What you are saying is that the Defence must allege that there is something within the Statute as it is provided that prevents him receiving a right to a fair trial, and we may examine that, but we may not examine the process by which the Security Council created the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am a little hesitant in saying it is restricted entirely to the parameters of the Statute. It is conceivable that somebody could point to something that happened in the process, but I cannot think of any.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not want to belabour it, but at some point today I am going to have to get a better understanding -- maybe my fellow judges can help me -- as to what your limits are. I am not suggesting you are not explaining them to me. I am telling you that I am just not understanding. What I want to know is based on what is on the table now, and what we have from the Defence are not challenges to anything that is in the Statute or even in our rules. It was interesting he raised the point about our provision for perjury matters, but in any case, he is not at this point challenging anything that is written in the Statute that somehow affects the right to a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am reluctant to leave this point until I have assisted your Honour with it. The Statute is a very, very good starting point because it reflects the very factors upon which you must act. If there is something in the Statute that would render it impossible for you to give a fair trial, then that is a very good starting point to look at that. The way around it may not be to say: "Well, the Security Council did not have the authority to create this Tribunal or anything at all". So it might be to say: "This is to be interpreted this way because to interpret it any way would be inconsistent with the rights of a fair trial and a fair trial must be rendered". That may be one way of resolving it. If it reached an absolute impediment to a fair trial, then one does not go on to say: "Well, the Security Council erred in the creation of the Tribunal or it did not have the capacity or power to create the Tribunal", it is not resolved that way. It is simply saying: "We cannot lend our jurisdiction to this trial because we have an overriding responsibility to ensure it is fair; if it is not fair, we cannot allow the trial to proceed". But it does involve an examination of what the Security Council said in that sense. One starts with the context of what is a fair trial. One goes out as far as it is necessary, examining what is raised by the Defence, one goes out as far as necessary to be satisfied that none of these issues preclude you, as a Tribunal, from rendering a fair trial. Once you are satisfied of that, that is the end of the examination. In my submission, merely being satisfied that it was created by the Security Council acting under Articles 41 and 39 Chapter VII is sufficient. That is the end of the matter. It may be that you do not need to go that far. Perhaps I am too generous. It may be to say the fact that the Security Council created is the end of the matter, but because it is a novel creation in a sense, and the Defence have rightly pointed to that, you may want to go just that little bit further so to satisfy yourselves that you can render a fair trial, and that is nothing in what they raise that would preclude you from doing that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Who can raise this issue? If the person who is subject to criminal responsibility cannot raise the issue here, who can raise it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Does your Honour mean how is it resolved at the end of the day if you cannot examine the decision?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is resolved this way. What you do is you say: "We decline to extend jurisdiction". That creates an impasse. It is for the political organs then to re-examine what they have done and make a determination of whether or not they are going to change it. They may choose not to change it, which means the Tribunal stops because no more cases can be brought before it. If it was such a fundamental issue that every time a case was brought this impediment precluded the ability to render a fair trial, but it is not for this Tribunal to go on and embark upon an examination of the organ that created it. If the requirement of providing a fair trial is the impediment that confronts you, you must stay the proceedings and then leave it to the political organs to resolve.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we would say then that we do not have jurisdiction to review, whether or not the Security Council acted arbitrarily or capriciously in the establishment, but we recognise that there should be a right of a review or, perhaps, we do not have to make that second statement. We do not have the jurisdiction to review. So, therefore, we just go home?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, what you say -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We tell the Security Council to do something that will satisfy someone and not come back to us again with a challenge to jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. What you say is: "We cannot proceed any further. So these proceedings will cease until such time as this impediment that has been raised" -- I keep saying, there is no impediment that has been raised -- "this impediment to our ability to render a fair trial is removed". It is not for the Tribunal -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But we would have to identify the impediment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In the process of identifying that impediment, we are reviewing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but in the context of deciding whether or not you can render a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Okay. If the Namibia case can be read as at least the International Court of Justice engaging in a limited review of the Security Council's powers in its issuing resolutions, if it can read that way, does that help to give us, this Tribunal, some limited power of review of the question of the establishment of this Tribunal by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the context of rendering a fair trial, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It helps us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the context of establishing whether or not you can render a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am going to leave you alone on that issue, I think, and make sure I have an understanding after I look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, furthermore, as the General Assembly has no adjudicatory power or authority to take coercive action, and as this criminal tribunal is both adjudicatory and takes coercive action, Article 22 of the Charter could not be used to create the Tribunal by the General Assembly, because the General Assembly cannot use Article 22 to give a subordinate body that it creates powers that it does not possess itself. Thus, Article 22 of the UN Charter does not authorise the General Assembly to create a Tribunal like this Tribunal. The appropriate Article is Article 29 which provides that the Security Council may establish such subsidiary organs as it deems necessary for the performance of its functions. In paragraph 2.4 the Defence suggest that the Tribunal could have been established by an amendment to the Charter of the United Nations. Articles 108 and 109 deals with this issue of amendment to the Charter. In order to secure an amendment to the Charter, such amendment requires the support of two-thirds of the General Assembly plus two-thirds ratification by member-states. The Charter has only been amended three times in its history, and all three amendments concern the increasing of membership numbers and related matters. Amendment to the Charter is a cumbersome and time-consuming process and not one that could be processed quickly, which was the requirement of the Security Council when the Tribunal was created. In any event, one must ask why would the Security Council go down the route of encouraging the General Assembly to seek an amendment of the Charter if it had available to it Chapter VII and Article 29? In the first sentence of paragraph 2.5 of the Defence motion, they say that the General Assembly is the most appropriate organ to confer jurisdiction on an international criminal court. They seek to obtain support for this proposition from a suggestion by the Islamic Conference that the General Assembly by resolution should approve the Statute of the Security Council which creates the Tribunal. In our submission, this suggestion does not support this proposition, that the General Assembly should confer jurisdiction on an international court. In any event, the fact that the Tribunal's budget is approved by the General Assembly in a practical sense achieves a measure of control over the Tribunal by the General Assembly. In this regard, it is worthy to note that this process of approval of the budget by the General Assembly, has already taken place at least in one instance. In paragraph 3.1 the Defence says -- I am paraphrasing -- that the establishment of the Tribunal by the Security Council is not a measure within the scope of Chapter VII of the Charter because the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina is not international. In response to this submission, the Prosecution makes four points: The first thing we say in our written submission that the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina is an international conflict. Mr. Fenrick will go into this in greater detail. Secondly, the action by the Security Council in establishing the Tribunal was based on the whole of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, and not just Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thirdly, sub-article 7 of Article 2 of the Charter makes it clear that Chapter VII action is not only limited to international disputes. Fourthly, that the justification for the taking of Chapter VII action is the threat to international peace and security, not whether the threat arises out of an international conflict. In paragraph 3.2.1 the Defence argue that the Article 41 list of measures do not include the establishment of a war crimes tribunal such as this Tribunal. However, Article 41's primary focus, in our submission, is to measures not involving the use of armed force. When contrasted with Article 42, which contemplates the use of force, the limiting influence, if it were, on Article 41 is not the list of measures contained in the Article but whether or not force was used. In any case, the Defence admit that the list of measures in Article 41 are not exhaustive. I raised these matters not so much as to encourage an examination of all these questions, but to answer the questions that have been raised by the Defence. In our submission, the achievement of international peace and security, especially through non-military means is such a desirable objective for the whole of mankind that the Security Council should not be constrained by a narrow interpretation of Article 41, but should be encouraged to explore novel and ingenious ways in which to bring about this consequence. In paragraphs 3.4.1. to 3.4.3, the Defence say that the Security Council should not be involved in the protection of humanitarian law because it requires the participation of a neutral body such as the International Committee of the Red Cross. However, if a party to a conflict participates in widespread abuse of human rights which in turn triggers a flood of refugees who spill over borders into neighbouring states, then it is readily understandable how the unsettling effect of having to cope with these refugees could have an effect on international peace and security such as to provoke Security Council action under Chapter VII.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Niemann, you need to slow down just a little bit, at least for me, and speak a little louder and, perhaps, for the court reporter, I do not know, but slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will do. In paragraph 3.5, the Defence say that the Tribunal cannot function as an independent judicial body if it is a subsidiary organ of the Security Council. However, the Prosecution submits, firstly, that the division of powers between an executive and a judiciary in a national set has much in common with this relationship between the Security Council and the Tribunal. In many national jurisdictions the judiciary is financially dependent upon the Executive, but provided the Executive respect the role of the judiciary, and vice versa, the dependency is not an obstacle to the independence and impartiality of the judiciary and, in the context of this Tribunal, we have such things as the independence of the judges, the independence of the Prosecutor and so forth. Secondly, if the Tribunal is controlled by a particular organ of the United Nations and, as I have referred to earlier, it is more the General Assembly because the budget is approved, the judges are appointed by the General Assembly and the President reports annually to both the Security Council and the General Assembly. In paragraph 3.6, the Defence debate whether or not the events in former Yugoslavia constitute an exceptional circumstance. Whatever the outcome of that debate might be, it in no way infringes upon the decision of the Security Council under Chapter VII to create the Tribunal as the existence of an exceptional circumstance is not relevant to the criteria. The relevant criteria is the threat to international peace and security.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you one moment? You said that you would discuss four points; whether there is an international conflict or, at least, Mr. Fenrick would discuss that; secondly, you said that it should be based on the whole of the conflict -- will Mr. Fenrick discuss that, because you just simply told us it should be and you did not really give us any authority and I did not recall seeing any in your brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I should address that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So I would like you to talk more about that. Then you spoke about threats to international peace being permissible if there are violations of international humanitarian law. You really did not speak very much about that. I am not sure whether that is something Mr. Fenrick is going to talk about, because I had some questions. Finally, are you going to talk about the impact of the Security Council resolution, because if you are, I have some questions about it, or if you are, I will wait until you begin to talk about; if you are not, I have some questions about it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was not going to talk about it, so it might be appropriate to talk about it now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you then. Regarding the Security Council resolutions, you say in your brief that the Security Council has applied grave breaches and they know, at least you say in your brief, that those apply to international conflicts. You also say, I think, that there were resolutions condemning the intervention by Croatia and Serbia, and because of this the Security Council has determined -- I may not be properly characterising fully, at least, your argument -- this is an international conflict. I guess my question to you is, do you really stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will not say whether or not we stand by it at this stage because it is a matter which Mr. Fenrick is going to address, and I do not want to touch upon it. I might just briefly respond to it by simply saying, without wishing to restrict Mr. Fenrick in any way, it is evidence of the fact that is how the Security Council responded to the situation, but I think I had better leave it to Mr. Fenrick. I am sorry. In relation to the whole of conflict, there is not much more I wish to say about that, other than the fact that the Statute of the Tribunal addresses itself to former Yugoslavia. So, in our submission, it is in no way to be found in the Statute an expression or a view by the Security Council when creating it that it wanted to limit it to any particular part. It is was the whole of the former Yugoslavia. That is the point in the context of the creation of the Tribunal. There is a different context when one talks about the particular offences -- and Mr. Fenrick will deal with that -- but in the context of creation of the Tribunal it is the whole of Yugoslavia. The threat to international peace, again that is another matter your Honour raised. I raised that and say simply this, that it is a political question and very hard for this Tribunal to determine whether or not that is, in fact, the case. I submit that it is not necessary for you to determine that, whether it was, in fact, a threat to international peace. The level of your examination, as I said earlier, relates to whether or not the creation of the Tribunal impacts upon the ability to provide a fair trial, etc. All I am submitting is that it is understandable why one could think that with refugees spilling over borders and events happening like this, this may in the minds of the Security Council -- if it is appropriate to speak of it in terms of having "minds" -- would constitute a threat to international peace and security to which they responded, but it is not a matter that I am encouraging your Honours to go into and to examine in any depth at all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can we even establish that because it is so fact based and because, perhaps, there is no definition of what constitutes a threat to peace?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Probably not, your Honour. But, in any event, you should not, in my submission, because it has nothing to do with whether or not you can provide for a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except that the Defence says that was an arbitrary, inconsistent decision taken by the Security Council. That is the predicate finding for the Security Council, I gather, to determine that it will create a measure to deal with this threat to peace, but that their very finding was arbitrary, just as arbitrary as saying that, well, it is arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it is arbitrary, your Honour -- I am not going to debate that it is not -- does that arbitrariness in any way impact on the ability of this chamber to provide for a fair trial?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, because we cannot provide for a fair trial for anyone because we are the result of an arbitrary establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, in my submission, it is not capricious. It is arbitrary in the sense that many things are arbitrary. The Prosecutor might bring one case ahead of another case. The Prosecutor might seek an adjournment for 10 days rather than five, all of that is arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that arbitrary and capricious?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I submit there is nothing to suggest it is capricious.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. You disagree on the merits, but is that something that we should look at, to determine whether it is arbitrary and capricious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, because it has not been raised. There is nothing that has been raised to suggest it is capricious.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Perhaps I do not understand the definition then of "capricious", but I had listened to the Defence yesterday and I thought that they were pretty strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. They made a good point but it was hypothetical and irrelevant. The good point was that white haired people should be prosecuted but, unfortunately, it does not assist them because that was not the decision of the Security Council. In paragraph 6.3 the Defence speak of the Tribunal invading domestic jurisdiction. However, the crimes contained within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal are universal in nature, and well recognised by international law, and had existed long before the creation of the Tribunal. Repression of such -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, did you say 6.3?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 6.3, your Honour. The Defence speak of invading domestic jurisdiction. However, the crimes contained within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal are universal in nature, they are well recognised by international law and existed long before the creation of the Tribunal. Repression of such crimes is certainly within the jurisdiction of nation states, but not exclusively so. If the Security Council elects to create its own Tribunal to share the burden of bringing the perpetrators of these universal crimes to justice, that can in no way be said to constitute an invasion of a state's jurisdiction because it was never the exclusive jurisdiction of an individual state in the first place. Your Honours, unless I can assist you in anything further -- I intended to be brief -- that was all I intended to say, but if there are any other matters that I may assist you with? Perhaps Mr. Fenrick could now proceed with his submission and perhaps I could come back if there are any other matters that occur to your Honours in relation to our submission. But other than that, we rely upon our written submission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the specific topics that I will be addressing are related to subject matter jurisdiction and, essentially, I would like to begin by reiterating, as we know, that the Tribunal was established as an ad hoc measure to provide a means for the Prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of former Yugoslavia. To use the words of the representative of New Zealand the during the Security Council debate when the Security Council resolution 827 was adopted: "The atrocities reportedly committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, notably in Bosnia and Herzegovina, have horrified and continue to horrify all of us. New Zealand considers that it is imperative that persons responsible for acts of 'ethnic cleansing', the forced expulsion of people, systematic rape, torture and murder are brought to trial and are punished. The establishment of the Tribunal by this resolution ensures that we have in place an effective mechanism to achieve these ends". Articles 1 through 5 of the Statute give the Tribunal the power to accomplish these ends. The first argument which I would like to counter on the part of the Defence was the argument that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction over grave breaches under Article 2 of the Statute because the armed conflict in Bosnia is internal. It is the submission of the Prosecution that the conflict in Bosnia is, in substance, an international armed conflict between Bosnia and, initially, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, subsequently the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and, as a result, the grave breach provisions referred to in Article 2 of the Statute do apply. Both the Defence and the Prosecution have agreed that classification of the conflict is, essentially, a legal issue. The factual basis, however, for the Prosecution argument is established by a number of public documents, which we have introduced together with our statement, and by the statement of James Gow, an expert witness for the Prosecution. Extracts of his statement are in document 101 which was passed with you. Determining the nature of the conflict in Yugoslavia is, indeed, a difficult task. In fact, determining the nature of virtually any modern conflict is a difficult task. To use the words of Dietrich Schindler, who is an eminent scholar who has done work in this particular area: "Experience shows that most of the armed conflicts today do not fit into a particular one of the various categories distinguished by the Conventions and Protocols, but contain elements of two or more categories. The question as to what rules of humanitarian law are applicable in a particular situation may, therefore, be rendered excessively difficult". If I may introduce a slight personal note, at the end of the summation by the Defence yesterday, they quoted a memorandum which I had written. I must say that this, perhaps, is a personal indication of how difficult the classification issue is. In fact, what happened was a colleague of mine published an extract of a memorandum which I had, indeed, written on the classification of the conflict issue. It shows up in page 299 of a book by Leslie Green entitled "The Contemporary Law of Armed Conflict". I hasten to add that, as indicated in the footnote, the particular memorandum which I was somewhat surprised to see quoted is dated 19th December 1992. Two and a half years have passed since that time. I must say, I like to think that my thinking on this topic has become somewhat more sophisticated in the meantime. I hasten to add there were also additional qualifications on the conclusions reached which do not appear in Professor Green's book. Our argument ------

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that a statement that you said that the conflict became internal after May?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The specific quotation -- I did not wish to over-emphasise it -- that after 19th May the conflict should be considered as internal, essentially, and that was based on work which had been done at that time, not on work which has been done since that time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then you were member of the Commission of Experts ---

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- I did not know that, but now you are a member of the Prosecution team?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sure you did not see the confirmation -- may be I should not even get into this -- hearings of Justice Clarence Thomas; he kind of ran into some of these things, you know, that he said when he was a member of the Executive and now he wants to be a member of the judiciary, he said ideas have changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I am sincerely hoping there is no personal aspect of this ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, no, just the change from when you are a member of the Executive working as Chairman of the Equal Employment Opportunities Commission and then, of course, you want to become a Justice, a Supreme Court Justice, maybe you change and you have changed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: In some respects, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But based on more information, that is really -----

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, the essential approach, our argument is that there is, indeed, more information, that at that particular point in time relatively little work had been done on the subject. Our approach is that one must look at the conflict in Bosnia in totality. If all we do is focus on bits and pieces or things that are happening in particular areas, we do, in fact, miss the wood for the trees. It is our assertion that there are a number of, essentially, uncontested facts and some contested assertions which can demonstrate the international nature of the conflict. On the basis of documentary evidence, we have established that Yugoslavia, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a successor state, was by general repute and its own admission actively involved through its military forces in the conflict in Bosnia until at least 19th May 1992. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia asserts that it withdrew its military forces from Bosnia-Herzegovina on or about 19th May. However, if we look at a statement made by the Minister of Defence of Yugoslavia at the time of the breakup, he stated in his own memoirs: "The units and headquarters of the JNA formed the back bone of the army of the Serb Republic with complete weaponry and equipment. That army with the possibility of calling upon its own people, if required, and with their total support, which is required in any modern war, protected Serb people and created military preconditions for an adequate political solution that would suit Serb national interests and goals to the extent, of course, that these are allowed by present international circumstances". That particular quotation is at page 41 in the Prosecution brief. Essentially, the JNA, together with its Bosnian Serb allies, conquered a very substantial portion of Bosnia. Then to a degree, disentangled itself or attempted to disentangle itself from the conflict. The Republic of Srpska Establishment Proclamation of 9th January 1992 states it is part of the federal state of Yugoslavia. The constitution adopted by the same entity on 28th February 1992 states it is part of the federal state of Yugoslavia and that its citizens hold both citizenship in the Republic of Srpska and Yugoslav citizenship. The FRY (the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia) continued to be a major source of logistical and financial support for the Bosnian Serb entity and its war effort after May 1992. It also continued to provide a degree of direct military support. On 22nd June 1992, Bosnia declared it was in a state of war as a result of aggression carried out by the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Montenegro, the Yugoslav Army and terrorists of the Serbian Democratic Party. It is our submission that when all of these factors are taken together, clearly, what we have is an international armed conflict existing in the territory of Bosnia between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia starting in April of 1992 and continuing at a minimum throughout the period covered by the various charges related to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, you say that the Yugoslav Army conquered Bosnia. Is not the situation at the beginning of 1992 that Bosnia was part of Yugoslavia, the army that was there was the national army? How was there any concept of conquest? It was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, it was at home, your Honour. It ceased to be at home as soon as Bosnia became an independent state. That independence process commenced early in 1992 and, at a minimum, was complete by early April 1992 when Bosnia was recognised by a number of foreign states. As of that point in time, the JNA, the Yugoslav Army, was no longer at home. At that point in time it should have withdrawn. It did not. It took part in an armed conflict which commenced at about that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So it became an army of occupation from that time, did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If we are going to look at spacial considerations, did that apply to the particular camp that we are considered with?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the fundamental argument is that although you can divide some aspects of this conflict up, you cannot divide up Bosnia and say ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: -- "You have a conflict here" or "You do not have one there". Bosnia is an independent state. This was a foreign army in Bosnia after, at most, early April 1992. Yes, it was an army of occupation and, yes, it applied to all of Bosnia, not part of it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Between April and May under whose control was the Prijedor region, do you know? There was fighting in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And certainly by May 19th the JNA withdrew?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: They WITHDREW approximately around that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Officially by name they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Which of these statements you have made can we accept as evidence, presumably, if there is authentication, which can we accept judicial notice of? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It is difficult to do that, your Honour, but my suggestion would be that the public documents are precisely that; that the constitutions of an establishment proclamation of the Serbian Republic, subsequently the Republic of Srpska, are things which one could take judicial notice of; the fact that different states recognised Bosnia, I think it would be possible to take judicial notice of. I would think that it is established that Yugoslavia was involved until, at least, 19th May on the basis of its own admissions. Some of the documents that were filed by the Prosecution I refer to contained references indicating Yugoslavia saying: "We have decided, we pull people out by 19th May". At a bare minimum, I think they were there until 19th May.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about the Minister of Defence's statement that you have quoted from?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It is a book your Honour. Certainly, the Prosecution submits it is something with very strong persuasive force. The nature of the breakup of the JNA in Bosnia, that is an assertion of ours which we believe could be adequately established in evidence and which we think is adequately substantiated in the statement of James Gow, extracts of which are appended to our brief in document 101 that was passed with the Prosecution brief.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, the Defence takes a different position with respect to the breakup. Their position is that the JNA then left portions of its equipment, material, to Serbians, some Croatians -- well, Serbians and Bosnians, and they took that. So their position is very different than yours regarding the break up, what happened after May 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So I suppose my concern is how can we then, if it is necessary (and that is something I am sure you will address) for us to determine whether it is international or internal, how we will determine what was the character of the conflict after May 19th, if we have to, and how can we determine what was the character of the conflict in the Prijedor region, if we have to? That seems to be based on information you have given us that is contained in Professor's Gow's statement. He will be a witness of yours ---

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- if we proceed to trial, then there will be an opportunity to cross-examine. I imagine the Defence may have witnesses, if they choose, of course, regarding this point, and then you will have an opportunity to cross-examine. We do not have that at this moment. We have two different positions, and it causes me some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. It would be our submission that what we have put in so far is sufficient for you to draw a conclusion that the conflict is international. Even if you strip away the parts where we appear to have a dispute with the Defence, I do not believe that the Defence is arguing that the Establishment Proclamation did not say that the Republic of Srpska or its citizens were citizens of Yugoslavia, I do not believe that they would assert that the constitution said anything other than what we say it says. I presume what we are really talking about is what happened on or about 19th May. That is a dispute. If that particular aspect is something which is essential to your determination, from our point of view, what we have said is sufficient, but perhaps you might decide that you need more at the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does it make a difference whether if the JNA departed on or about May 19th -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Fenrick, can I ask you this? It is really your case, is it not, that the Bosnian Serb notification of the fact that it is part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia means that the international conflict that you identified as existing until the withdrawal of the Federal Republic's army continued on, continued on in the guise of a part of the Federal Republic, namely, the Serbian element in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is what makes it international.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Then you say, rather sweepingly, and we need worry about beast pieces of Bosnia, it is an international conflict affecting the whole territory, at least the territory that is occupied by this portion of the Federal Republic, namely the Serbian element in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, and I contain to maintain that sweeping approach, your Honour. When a country is engaged in an international armed conflict, the entire country is engaged. You does not have some provinces or some opstinas involved and others not involved. It is a country by country process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I think I understand how you put it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When the JNA then left -- a lot of this perhaps is evidence that will have to be adduced at trial and, if we get to that point, we will talk about it -- had Prijedor then fallen under the control of first the FRY and then the Bosnian Serbs by May 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Roughly in that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Certainly before the JNA left, the persons who were residing in that area were persons -- perhaps we will get to that point -- who were protected by the grave breaches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When the JNA then leaves, does that mean that they no longer have that protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It is our argument, your Honour, that considered in totality you have got a continuing conflict even if you have a nominal withdrawal of the JNA

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: They have left behind an entire army and Serbia is -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that but I am on to something else now. I understand your position, I understand Defence. But let us assume that we cannot resolve at this point, at least in the state of the record, what JNA did with its material, etc.. We just cannot decide whether it was evenly distributed or whether or not it really went to the Serbs totally. Suppose we cannot decide that, do we have to decide that, if we decide, based upon matters about which we can take judicial notice, that the JNA was there until on or about May 19th, that Prijedor was under the control no longer of Bosnia-Herzegovina but under the control of the JNA? Certainly at that point those persons who were there, if any violations occurred of the grave breaches, were to be protected, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What happens then, just as a matter of law, when the party leaves? Do all of a sudden those persons become not protected because there is no longer any presence of that international force that triggered their protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think our argument would be twofold in connection with that. One, that the mere fact that the armed conflict has ceased does not mean that the Geneva Conventions cease to apply. Once they are triggered, they continue to run. From our point of view, it would continue to apply in this area even after a nominal withdrawal. The second aspect of our argument is, in fact, related to the various agreements which have been entered into between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnia government and the Bosnia Croats. In fact, it would be the view of the Prosecution that you have, although it is assembled in a rather strange fashion, essentially, a seamless web. Either what you have is a conflict which may have some internal aspects, but all the parties to it have entered into binding agreements, pursuant to common Article 3, to apply the Geneva Conventions including implicitly the grave breach provisions, or you have an international armed conflict because of the extent of Yugoslav involvement and, just in case we needed a backup, it is also our submission that when the JNA pulled out that did not mean the end of the period of application of the Geneva Conventions in totality. In other words, it is our submission that there is enough there and, perhaps, the ensemble approach which we have been referring to must include those supplementary agreements as well as what the factual assertions that we have made. But it is our submission that there is enough that one could come to a conclusion across the board that the Geneva Conventions apply for a variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But as to the first then, from April through May 19th, 1992, if they were triggered because of the presence of the JNA, the ---

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- SFRY, then the protections were triggered then, and even though they may leave on May 19th, and even though they may divide their material as per the Defence's position, still the persons who were there are subject to the protections of the grave breaches because they were triggered during their presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is our argument, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But can I ask you, I do not quite follow that argument, if hostilities ceased at that stage, that would not be your argument, would it? The Convention itself as distinct from occupied territory talks of the provisions coming to an end once hostilities cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: There are different provisions in the different treaties, your Honour. In the case of the Prisoners of War Convention, it is when the prisoners are turned back, for example. For the Civilians Convention, if occupation is -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I was thinking of Convention IV.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Convention IV, as indicated at page 42 of our brief, continues to apply until the general close of military operations. That is the final end of all fighting, and I do not think we have had that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But did you not have that at -- I see, only if you adopt the locality test that I think the Defence puts forward in Prijedor certainly fighting had ceased?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct, but it is ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But you say you cannot split up the country in that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It is our submission that is a legally untenable argument your, Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about the Defence's and you mentioned the declaration of war. Yesterday the Defence said that in June, was it, 1992 when Bosnia-Herzegovina declared itself to be in a state of war with the SFRY, at that point Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have control of the Prijedor region, so they certainly could not have been, from the Defence's point of view, saying: "In so far as that region is concerned, we are at war with SFRY", or did I misunderstand?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That may have been the Defence contention, your Honour. Our contention, however, is Bosnia is a state which includes all of the area of Bosnia. It is a member of the United Nations. Its state territory includes all of the boundaries that were there in the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You do not have another entity exercising statehood over that area , except to the extent it is an occupied power. But if France was at war in World War I and the fact that part of France was occupied, that did not mean that all of France was not at war.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would it mean that the area that was occupied then was a part of a de facto state of another party?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
