utterances.text: That would not be our submission, your Honour. Our submission is the whole territory is Bosnia unless and until there is a point in time when there are agreements made which alter that in some kind of a peace settlement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Croatia has been recognised -- does Croatia have a seat at the UN?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does Bosnia-Herzegovina have a seat at the UN?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does the SFRY have a seat at the UN?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: There is a seat for Yugoslavia in the UN. There is some confusion (and I am not sure what the present state of things are) as to precisely who sits in that seat.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do the Bosnian Serbs have a seat in the UN?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: No, they do not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, in so far, I guess, as the United Nations is concerned, what can we draw from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That the state is Bosnia; that the territory of Bosnia is all of the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina when it was a member of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even including the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: At some point, I do not know, lines may shift, they might have control one day and might not have control another day, but regardless of that the original boundaries then -----

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: They are the legitimate government of the entire area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One final question on this point: Is there some inconsistency between what you have just been saying and your reliance on the fact that the Bosnian Serb state declared itself part of Yugoslavia? You say that it is all Bosnia, but at the same time you say: "But, look, here the Bosnian Serbs have declared themselves part of the Federal State of Yugoslavia".

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It is our submission that there is no real inconsistency, your Honour. What we have is a group in a state who have declared that they belong to another state. It does not mean that the state does not continue to exist. If, for example, in Belgium one part of the population for some reason decided that it wanted to belong to Germany and announced it belonged to Germany, it does not mean that Belgium is not Belgium and Belgium does not have the same boundaries as before. All it means is that one group in the country has claimed that it has allegiance to and belongs to this other state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps I misunderstood you, but I thought you were putting it that there was a continuation of the presence of Yugoslav troops in Bosnia because the Bosnian Serbs had said they were part of Yugoslavia and, therefore, the part of the army that went over to them was, in fact, the Yugoslav army and, therefore, there was an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It is our argument, your Honour, that what you have is a group of people who live in the territory of the state of Bosnia. That group of people is very closely linked to Yugoslavia to such an extent that they can be considered, essentially, an extension of Yugoslavia. The fact that you have an extension because of what the people have said does not necessarily mean the territory has changed into something else. I would also submit, your Honour, that this approach is reinforced to a degree by the approach taken by various organs of the United Nations, in particular, the Security Council. I believe you had some questions about that and the weight to be assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The question I had was, has the Security Council unequivocally stated that the conflict is an international conflict, one, and if they have not said explicitly but because of its application, application of the grave breaches to the conflict, should we then draw the conclusion that it is international? You say in your brief they should be given -- I am not sure whether you say great weight, you say "weight", but I am not sure of exactly the line. So, tell me, what effect are the resolutions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if what we were talking about was a case concerned with a different period in time, for example, one which arose or where the facts arose after the Tribunal was established, it might be that a different argument would be advanced, but what we are talking about now is a situation which occurred before the Tribunal was established. For that reason, it is the approach of the Prosecution that we must establish on a factual basis that either an international armed conflict existed at that point in time, or for some other reason, such as the agreements under common Article 3, the parties have agreed to apply the law for international armed conflict. It is our view that it would be appropriate to assign weight -- indeed, we would say great weight -- to the determinations of the Security Council, but we do not assert that the Security Council has purported to make a binding decision at any time prior to the establishment of the Tribunal that the conflict in the former Yugoslavia is international. It would implicitly certainly have appeared to have considered it international on many occasions in many of the resolutions which it has passed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If we put that into the pot, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What effect does the presence of Croatia have on the character of this conflict? Sometimes Croatia has been in an armed conflict with Muslims and at other times they have been together. Is that so? Does that make a difference or do we have to isolate the time and isolate the geographic area?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is my understanding that under the traditional law, if what we are considering is the situation in Bosnia exclusively, if you have a non-international armed conflict, presumably, for some reason you decided that the conflict was between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Serbs alone and was not an international armed conflict, then the addition of Croatian forces to the Bosnia government forces, i.e. coming to the assistance of the established government, does not convert that into an international armed conflict. On the other hand, if an external force joined another country, joined with the Bosnian Serb group (as indeed we have maintained Yugoslavia has), then a foreign state assisting a group of rebels (if they are classified as that) that is sufficient to change it. So, simply put, addition of Croatia does not really change the situation where we are concerned here. I would just like to continue briefly, your Honour: As we have asserted, the variety of agreements which the parties have entered into in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina have, from our point of view, converted what may be a conflict with some internal aspects into a conflict where the bulk of international humanitarian law for international armed conflicts does apply including the grave breach provisions. We rest a considerable amount of weight on, particularly, the May 22nd 1992 agreement and also, to assist us in interpreting it, a subsequent agreement concluded on October 1st, 1992, concerning release and transfer of prisoners. It is our submission that these agreements are, as the Defence has conceded, or rather as the Defence has recognised the possibility of agreements under common Article 3 to bring in the rest of law of armed conflict, it is our submission that that is, in fact, what these agreements have done. We would add on top of those agreements, of course, the London declaration signed by Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Boban and Mr. Karadzic at the London conference on August 27th, 1992. It is our submission that these agreements carried out or drafted under the auspices of the International Committee of the Red Cross and the either unilateral declarations or additional legally binding treaties entered into by the three political leaders in London are sufficient to apply the law for international armed conflict to the conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With respect to May 22nd 1992 agreement, that specifically excluded, well, it did not specifically exclude the grave breaches, but it does not include them, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because of articles 13 -- it does not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But you are saying then that common Article 3, as a matter of customary international law, is included by virtue of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: No, your Honour. This is not the common Article 3 argument, if I might. That is something that I would intend to make at a slightly later point. The argument is that these are agreements concluded pursuant to common Article 3 ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: -- so that parties engaged in what is a conflict with some internal aspects can agree to apply the remainder of the law. It is our argument that, notwithstanding the absence of an explicit reference to the grave breach provisions in the May 22nd agreement, implicitly the parties must have agreed to apply the grave breach provisions for the simple reason that at a later point in time, when they concluded an agreement on release and transfer of prisoners, they included a provision in the prisoner exchange agreement saying: "All prisoners not accused of or sentenced for grave breaches of international humanitarian law will be unilaterally and unconditionally released". They would have no need for a provision like that in a prisoner exchange agreement concluded in October if the earlier agreement was not something which, at least implicitly, allowed for the prosecution of persons for grave breaches. Further to that, the May 22nd agreement, although it did not explicitly refer to the grave breaches, also contained provisions in Article 5 whereby there was an obligation to punish violations of the agreement. The violations are, in fact, the grave breaches. That is our submission, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not recall the Defence really addressing this, but can it be looked at as an explicit intention on the part of the parties not to include the grave breaches? They are going to list various articles. Why list the Articles if they intend to apply all of the convention?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: The argument is not that they intend to apply all of the Conventions, your Honour. What you have is a number of substantive obligations they have agreed to; "We Will do this, we will do that, we will do this". At the end you have in Article 5 an agreement: "If we do not do these things we, will punish the people who are responsible for it".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Where is that? I am not following that part. I see. You are referring to the agreement itself, Article 5, Implementation?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, your Honour, I was indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you are saying Article 5, the Implementation section, picks up the grave breaches?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then the London conference, you say that there they say that the parties agreed to be bound to comply with their obligations under international humanitarian law and, in particular, Geneva Conventions of 1949 and additional protocols. You are saying that is to be interpreted as an agreement to be bound to the grave breaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I do, your Honour. Of course, continuing on that line it says "... and that persons who commit or order the commission of grave breaches are individually responsible". It is the submission of the Prosecution that either this plan of action of August 1992 and the supplementary agreements of May 22nd and October 1st have meaning or they do not. We must presume that these commitments were entered into knowingly by the people who entered into them, and that they intended and deliberately bound the people for whom they were responsible to comply with the grave breach provisions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That was in August, August 27th 1992. That is beyond the date of offences covered in the indictment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that alone would not be sufficient to establish an agreement to be bound by grave breaches which you could thus apply in the indictment; is that not so? This alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. Our assertion is that this is, essentially, a reaffirmation and a recognition and a restatement of existing obligations. From the point of view of the Prosecution, the primary binding legal document is the May 22nd agreement. A legitimate means of interpretation of the May 22nd agreement is the Prisoner Exchange Agreement concluded later on in the year, where the parties agreed among themselves that they would not hand back prisoners who were charged with or imprisoned for grave breaches. There would be no need for such a provision at all if they had not already had an understanding among themselves that persons committing grave breaches were to be punished.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Need we find that the conflict was international if the parties agree to bind themselves to the grave breaches?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: No. There is no need to find that the conflict is international in this particular case. What, perhaps, is a particularly appropriate approach would be to decide that in so far as Yugoslavia is involved the conflict is international; in so far as the conflict has internal aspects, these agreements concluded by the parties to that internal conflict are sufficient to bind those parties too to comply with the grave breach provisions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then the last one, you want us to hold the lawyer to his statement before the International Court of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes. Unless you have further questions concerning the argument related to Article 2 of the Statute, your Honour, I would propose to move on and discuss prosecution under Article 3.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One other question. In your brief, you stated -- I think you stated -- that you considered Mr. Tadic to be a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I am not sure if we stated that, your Honour, but I think that would be our view.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does it make any difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: He certainly resides in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does it make any difference or do we need to focus on where the alleged offences were committed?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: No, I think all we are concerned with, your Honour, is where the offence occurred. The nationality of somewhere committing a grave breach is normally irrelevant except that they should have links to one side of the conflict while the victim should have links to the other.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yesterday we talked a little bit about a possibility of stipulations. I do not know really how to explore that. Perhaps the parties can get together, except you understand that we are anxious to resolve both of these two motions and to enter into certain stipulations of fact that you are able to; if you are not able to do, we will do what we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did have a prepared statement in this regard. I think we would be interested in discussing the possibility of stipulations with you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is something then you will do outside the presence of the judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Certainly. The particular statement that we wish to read concerning the factual allegations was that most of the arguments that we are making here clearly concern questions of law exclusively, but when what we are talking about is the classification argument, one aspect of that, the one about whether or not it really is an international armed conflict, is one which depends upon factual underpinnings, although it is our assertion that it is primarily a legal argument. The Prosecution submits that it has established these foundational facts by means of documentary evidence and the affidavit of an expert witness. The Prosecution further submits that this evidence considered in totality is sufficient to establish the international character of the conflict beyond any question. We can (and will) discuss the possibility of stipulations further with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One other question: With respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina acceding to the Geneva Convention, you say that was done in, whenever, November but backdated to June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Backdated to 6th March.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: March 1992. You say also that the SFRY then ratified the Geneva Conventions in 1950. I gather by that you are meaning, and then you cite, I think, the Vienna Convention on succession or something. So you are saying there that the SFRY is a successor state to the former Yugoslavia ---

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- or are all of the republics that were at one point a part of Yugoslavia successors and, if so, then why do you even need to refer to Bosnia-Herzegovina acceding to the requirements of the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: There is a provision in the Vienna Convention on state succession or succession to treaties which, essentially, provides that if a state breaks up, the legal obligations which applied in the territory before the breakup continue to apply until such point in time as the new state decides whether or not it wishes to be bound by the treaty, or make some positive indication it does not wish to be bound by the treaty. Our argument is that, regardless of whether or not Bosnia had, in fact, gone on and ratified the additional Protocols and the Geneva Conventions, the Geneva Conventions and the Protocols would have continued to apply from the moment of the breakup until any point in time when it indicated that it did not want to be a party to the conventions. Of course, it has never indicated that. In the case of SFRY, I have been informed by the International Committee of the Red Cross that they view the present Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as being bound by the original ratifications by the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If that is such a clear argument written in stone somewhere, why are we are arguing or why are you two arguing over whether or not this is an international or internal conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: No, there is no question -- I am sure I have not made myself clear enough here -- the argument is not, do the treaties apply to the area; that, there is no question about, they clearly do apply. However, the Geneva Conventions (which is what we are specifically concerned with here) do not begin to apply in totality until they are triggered. The trigger is either the existence of an international armed conflict or some agreements pursuant to common Article 3 in the event of an internal arme conflict. That is what we are arguing about.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are correct, I am sorry, I misspoke. We were talking about the statement of Professor Gow that you have submitted. Is that in affidavit form? Declaration form?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I am informed it is a witness statement; it is not sworn to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Certainly, if you wish the Chamber to accept that, I imagine it should be sworn to as an affidavit, except then we have problems about the admissibility of certain things in the statement, do we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except the Tribunal does not have to worry about hearsay, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: We do not believe so, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: If I might, your Honour, the approach that is taken by the Prosecution, of course, and, as I understand, also by the Defence is, essentially, we are making legal argument here rather than trying to prove facts. Having said that, obviously with the factual underpinnings at issue, there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am not balking at you or the Defence; I am just telling you the dilemma that we are in trying to make a determination, if we have to, as to whether it is international or internal and then giving some support.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Do you wish me to move on to the next argument?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: The next argument, your Honour, has to do with the power of the Tribunal to prosecute the accused under Article 3 of the Statute for committing violations of the laws or customs of war in an armed conflict. The Defence has asserted that the Tribunal has no power to prosecute under Article 3 of the Statute for violations of the laws and customs of war in internal conflicts.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you move on to that, I did not realise you were leaving grave breaches. What position do you take with respect to the US amicus curiae that we need not decide whether it was international or internal conflict, that the Geneva Conventions would apply anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: We find it an interesting and novel approach, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do not want to speak to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do not want to speak to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do not want to take a position one way or the other -- you do not have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I would rather not, no. The Defence asserts that the Tribunal has no power to prosecute under Article 3 of the Statute for violations of the laws and customs of war in internal conflicts. The Prosecution disagrees. The approach which is taken by the Prosecution on this issue is that Article 1 of the Statute sets out the competence of the Tribunal in general, and under Article 1 the Tribunal has the power to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law. International humanitarian law includes the rules which are applicable in both internal and international armed conflict. Serious violations of international humanitarian law can, therefore, include violations which occur in non-international armed conflicts. The question then is, assuming that that is correct (and we submit it certainly is) can a violation committed in an internal armed conflict fit into one of the heads in Articles 2 through 5 of the Statute? Clearly, that sort of violation would not fit under Articles 2, 4 or 5. The question then is, does it, can it, should it, be included under Article 3 of the Statute which refers to violations of the laws or customs of war?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You just took a position with respect to the amicus brief -----

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: No, I am sorry. Your Honour, my argument with respect or my non-argument with respect to the amicus brief on that particular issue was that we had some concerns about an argument that grave breaches could be committed in an internal armed conflict upon the basis of the argument put forth in the American brief. Our argument here is different. That was an argument related to Article 2 of the Statute. What we are arguing about here is Article 3 of the Statute. We are not suggesting that the violations of the laws or customs of war in internal armed conflict are grave breaches. We are suggesting that they fit in under Article 3. The basis for our argument is that, first of all, the expression "laws or customs of war" considered in the abstract, although at one point in time it referred exclusively to international armed conflicts, has evolved. Today, that concept, that expression, is something which applies to both international and internal armed conflicts. It does not have the same content in both types of conflict, but there is an existing concept of laws or customs of war, and that existing concept applies to both types of conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say in your brief that it does not have the same content. What do you mean by that; that there are certain laws and customs of war enumerated in the Hague Convention that all of them may not fit within common Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do not tell us which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Essentially, what we are putting forward right now is an argument that we are trying to prosecute for an unspecified violation in Article 3 of the Statute. Generally speaking, for international armed conflicts, you have a wide range of treaty obligations and customary law -- all kinds of stuff -- the whole Geneva Conventions, hundreds of pages, the additional protocols, the Hague regulations, quite a substantial mound of treaty material. For internal armed conflicts, what you have is a much reduced body of law. Part of that much reduced body of law is common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. There is also Protocol 2, which we are not referring to particularly in this argument. There is a provision in the Hague Cultural Property Convention. But the body of law which applies to internal armed conflict is a much more skeletal body than the body which applies to international armed conflict. What our argument is, is that some of, most of, certainly at least common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions can be classified as laws or customs of war in internal armed conflict. That is what we are hinging the argument on right here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then we look at common Article 3 and that lists certain offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But then, of course, in The Hague Convention there is a longer list of offences. What you are saying is if you put them side by side, you are not saying that all, but you are saying that only those that are listed in a common Article 3 would be included?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, at another point in time we might be arguing that additional provisions are included in that body of customary law applicable to internal armed conflicts, but at this point in time we are rooting our argument entirely in common Article 3.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just what is listed there?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes. Our argument is twofold: First of all, that there is this body of customary law for internal armed conflicts. Secondly, that the statements of the Security Council at the time the Statute was adopted clearly indicate that Article 3 of the Statute is intended to embrace all of the treaty obligations applicable to the territory of the former Yugoslavia, including, depending on the circumstances, both of the additional protocols and common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. In our written brief, we did, of course, lay out those various statements made by members of the Security Council. It is the submission of the Prosecution that those statements constitute an essential part of the legislative history of the Statute. As I am sure you are aware, if one reads the Secretary General's report in relation to Article 3 of the Statute, there is reference to virtually nothing but Hague law, the Hague Conventions of 1907. It is our submission that the Security Council, as a legislative body, gave meaning to the term "laws or customs of war" when it adopted that Statute, and that the meaning attached to it or the comments made by the Secretary General in the report which came out before the Security Council considered the Statute are, essentially, overtaken by events. The real meaning is found in the terms themselves "violations of the laws or customs of war" and in the interpretation, the uncontested interpretation, given to these terms by the members of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is adopting the generous American approach to legislative history. Do you suggest we should adopt that or that we should adopt a more orthodox common law approach or neither?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that one of two approaches would accomplish the objective that we have proposed. One is, what do the words mean all by themselves? In that case, our submission is that "violations of the laws or customs of war" includes a small group of customary law offences which occur in internal armed conflict as well as those which occur in international armed conflict; or one can pay heed, adopt the American approach concerning legislative history. Either of them is a satisfactory base, from our point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have not gathered what the foundation of the first approach is. Where do you get the authority for this small group of offences which apply to internal war?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: What we have done, your Honour, in connection with that is we have moved on somewhat and, essentially, what we have been doing is pinning our position on the Nicaragua case before the International Court of Justice which, of course, refers to common Article 3 as containing a minimum yardstick, sort of, a basic set of rules which apply to both international and internal armed conflict regardless of classification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If I may speak for the American way of interpreting Statutes, I am not sure whether -- well, I do not know. Normally, what you would do is you would look at the legislative history of what our congressmen say back and forth, back and forth, in order to determine what the meaning of an ambiguous Statute is -- I do not know whether it is ambiguous or not. At first, I was thinking that it was not ambiguous because of what the Secretary General said, clearly, that it would apply in Hague situations. But perhaps he is now just another piece of the interpretation. In other words, the Statute says "violating the laws or customs of war". It does not saying anything about "in armed conflict". He is one piece of the legislative history and the Security Council members are other pieces, I gather. That is what you are saying; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is exactly what we are saying, that the interpretation given in the Secretary General's report is not overriding or determinative.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But in order then to accept what the Security Council members said, do we not have to find then that common Article 3 has become a part of customary international law and that it is the minimum? You are now citing Nicaragua for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That is exactly what we are submitting; that Nicaragua provides an adequate basis for a conclusion by you that common Article 3 is part of customary law and is something that can fit in under this heading of "violations of the laws or customs of war". We would go further, in fact, your Honour. Our submission would be that in connection with that particular charge or, rather, in connection with common Article 3, or the rules contained in common Article 3, because those rules apply across the entire spectrum of conflict, because they apply to both international and internal armed conflict, if what you have is a charge related to one of the numbered heads in common Article 3, in fact, there is no need to determine classification of the conflict at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But you are addressing yourself to Article 3 of our Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: How do you link common Article 3 of the Convention? What persuasive force does that have on us in interpreting article 3 of our Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Article 3 of the Statute clearly indicates that there are other violations which can be punished. It says: "The International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons violating the laws or customs of war. Such violations shall include, but not be limited to", and our argument here is that common Article 3 is one of the "not be limited to" provisions, that it comes in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I follow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except as to this legislative history and whether the Statute is even vague, all of these offences that are listed come from the Hague Convention, do they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So it is not like they were picking from The Hague Convention and then picking from the common Article 3? I have not matched them closely. Then you have the Security Council members saying: "Oh, yes, include common Article 3". I think it is pretty clear to me, perhaps, that when this was written they were thinking about The Hague Convention, because that is what they listed. I suppose what happened is that the Security Council members told the Secretary General he was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: We, indeed, would suggest that, your Honour. It is -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But they did not change the words?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: They did not the change the text at any point, your Honour. My understanding is that what happened was the Secretary General's report, together with a Statute, a draft Statute, arrived before the Security Council. There was extended discussion but no tampering whatsoever with the words. You then have the Statute being adopted and a number of interpretive statements being made. I have no idea why there was no changing of the words, but one presumes that a substantial amount of weight should be assigned to the interpretive statements, particularly when there are, in fact, several members of the Security Council, several permanent members, commenting on this and the point is not contested.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The only thing that they could have changed because you have the words "such violations shall include", so that is include, that maybe enough, the only thing they could change would have been to pick some of the acts that are listed in common Article 3 and add them to the wording of Article 3 as another specific "including", you know, it ends in (e), they could have said (f), and they could have then picked up "outrages upon personal dignity, in particular, humiliating and degrading treatment".

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, they could have, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is unlikely to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It is submitted that, in fact, laws or customs of war is a very general term of art. If one reviews military manuals, for example, grave breaches are referred to often enough as violations of the laws or customs of war or war crimes. The expression itself is not arbitrarily confined to The Hague law exclusively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I suppose it is right also to say that war is not necessarily international war, is it? Civil war is war or not -- if one is going by the black lettered text.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, certainly one can adopt a variety of approaches there, your Honour. In fact, I believe that the American manual 27-10, The Law of Land Warfare Manual, lists violations of common Article 3 as "war crimes". In fact, there would probably be several other national manuals which would make the same sort of assertion. "War", when one is talking about "war crimes", has become a somewhat more open term. At one point in time, quite clearly, "war" meant declared war between two or more states. Declared wars have gone out of fashion. I do not know when the last time was that we had a declared war, but we still have war crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In any case, the Statute gives us jurisdiction to try violations, serious violations, of international and humanitarian law that are a part of customary international law; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is our submission, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And gives common Article 3 as a part of customary international law. We have jurisdiction over that and the Defence may agree with you in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Our submission is we look at Article 1, it fits in there, it is a serious violation of humanitarian law, and then we can fit it in under Article 3.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You were talking about the Nicaragua case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How does that make common Article 3 applicable to an international setting? Is that because the United States could only have been held responsible, if their relationship vis-a-vis Nicaragua was international, and yet they found that the United States had somehow encouraged violations of common Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: My understanding, your Honour, is that in the Nicaragua case, because the United States was not present to argue, the court was trying to find a customary law basis for a lot of things. Obviously, the United States was bound by the Geneva Conventions, as was Nicaragua and, as a result of that, obviously they were both bound by common Article 3. My understanding is that the approach that was taken by the court was that they deliberately wanted to identify a range of law which applied across the entire conflict spectrum and, for that reason, they focused on common Article 3. They did not say: "Common Article 3 applies to international armed conflict". What they did say, if I remember correctly, was: "The rules contained in common Article 3 constitute a minimum yardstick which applies to both international and internal conflicts and, as a result, we have no need to determine what the nature of the conflict is. We can just say: 'These Rules independent of their source and common Article 3 just apply all the time'".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can this Tribunal solve the dilemma that we are in right at this point by making such a finding with respect to Article 3? I do not know, you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It would be our submission that, yes, you could, your Honour, with respect to Article 3. If I could put in a qualifier there; it is our submission that if what we are talking about are the rules contained in common Article 3, those specific prohibitions, it would be the submission of the Prosecution that those Rules apply and can be fitted under Article 3 of our Statute independent of the classification issue. It would be desirable to avoid reference to common Article 3 itself except purely as a descriptive term, but there are a list of prohibited acts in common Article 3. If those prohibited acts are put in under Article 3 of our Statute, it would be the submission of the Prosecution that there is no need to determine the classification with reference to those particular acts. Unfortunately, the problem is not entirely solved there. It is solved with reference to common Article 3, but our argument would be that if we are talking about other things, as I said before, "laws or customs of war" is a term which applies to both international and internal armed conflict, but it does not have the same content both times. So, if we are talking about the itemised offences, for example, which are listed in Article 3 of our Statute, for some of those we probably still would have to classify the conflict as international or internal, but for common Article 3, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, apart from the United States, the United Kingdom and France, have other states indicated that the obligations of common Article 3 are included in Article 3 of the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: No. There was no comment on that issue by any other members of the Security Council, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, you may proceed. You are not finished with this argument though, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: We are getting close. If I might, what I wanted to go on to and talk about was in connection with common Article 3, in particular. It is our submission that at most what is happening here is the court is exercising jurisdiction over well-established existing offences. We are not creating new offences here. Under common Article 3 itself or, rather, under the provisions in the Geneva Conventions there is an obligation to suppress breaches, and states have an obligation to implement those treaty requirements. So it would be our submission that here we, in fact, have got something which is not a new offence, we are not offending the nullum crimen principle in any way whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think you referred to Professor Meron's Article regarding the universality of Article 3. Is that what you are saying, that there is a growing trend now to believe that common Article 3 contains that universality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Indeed, that is precisely what we were pointing at.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Professor Meron has written a lot about the Tribunal and he is very well-respected. Is there anyone else who agrees with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I -- yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am not suggesting there has to be; it is because he has written so much on it and so well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It is a topic which, by and large, people have not devoted sustained thought to. You will find a number of articles elsewhere, not referring to the problems of Tribunal, but elsewhere in general, which especially say: "No, you cannot prosecute" or "A state outside cannot prosecute for a violation of common Article 3". In fact, there is an article by Professor Rowe on "War Crimes in the former Yugoslavia, the legal difficulties", in 32 Military Law and Law of War Review 1993, at pages 317 to 360. Professor Rowe is one of those who is opposed to the idea of us having jurisdiction over common Article 3 offences. This is something which has not been reasoned through before, by and large. If one does reason it through, in fact, the end conclusion is perfectly reasonable, although it is not something which people have been focusing on in the past. Of course, there is no precedent for a tribunal like ours, and nation states by and large have no particular interest in prosecuting people who have committed offences in internal conflicts outside their own territory. So, it is a bit different but it is not unacceptable -- it does not cross any legal parameter. One would suspect that there may well, in fact, be more articles adopting a position similar to Professor Meron's, but it is not a well explored area in the literature, in general.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why is there a requirement, well, why do you argue the universality principle applies to common Article 3? Is it to respond to ex post facto the nullum crimen sine lege we have talked about? I only took two years of Latin. If I had known that I would be here, I am sure I would have taken many more years. But is that why? Is that the relationship?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is part of it, your Honour, but the court has to have a basis for exercising jurisdiction. The normal basis for exercising jurisdiction over things like grave breaches is universal jurisdiction. That is one reason why or, excuse me, the normal basis for exercising jurisdiction over things like war crimes and grave breaches outside the country where the conflict is occurring is universality. So that is certainly one basis that we wish to argue is usable by this Tribunal here. However, we would submit that, in fact, we have jurisdiction on more than that principle alone. We have been created by the Security Council for a purpose, prosecuting serious violations of international humanitarian law. That link to our Security Council mandate all by itself is, we would submit, also quite adequate to permit us to prosecute violations of common Article 3. Unless you have any further questions in connection with the common Article 3 argument, your Honour, I would propose to move on to Article 5 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I did have a question regarding page 52 of your brief. The second full paragraph at the end. Earlier you talked about Professor Meron's article and then later you say: "Consequently, the competence to create an international tribunal cannot be based upon existing International Humanitarian Law itself but, in the present case, upon Resolution 808". Then, of course, you cite the International Committee for the Red Cross. What do you mean by that? Is that what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is, essentially, exactly what I just said, your Honour, that, in fact, literally one would suppose that the universality concept is something which is normally exercised by states trying cases, and we are something different here. This Tribunal is a creature o the Security Council and it is exercising jurisdiction on a number of powers, on a number of bases.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: The argument of the Defence is that crimes against humanity as referred to in Article 5 of the Statute requires a nexus with international armed conflict. The Prosecution disagrees. It is our submission that under current customary law, crimes against humanity do not require any nexus at all with armed conflict. The Security Council has in Article 5 clearly imposed a requirement for a nexus with armed conflict. It is certainly perfect entitled to do so, but that requirement is narrower than the traditional international law definition of crimes against humanity. For that reason, it is the submission of the Prosecution that Article 5 is well within the boundary of the criteria for crimes again humanity and does not breach in any way the nullum crimen principle. The Defence relies to a considerable extent on the Statute of the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg. It is our submission that that Tribunal was deliberately given a limited jurisdiction over crimes against humanity because it was also an ad hoc tribunal and its purpose was the "just and prompt trial of the major war criminals of the European Axis". There are other legal documents, Control Council Law No. 10, for example, did not impose a requirement for a nexus with international conflict. Neither do documents, subsequent documents, such as the Convention on the Non-Applicability of Statutory Limitations to War Crimes and Crimes Against Humanity, the Genocide Convention and the Apartheid Convention. Since 1954 the International Law Commission has expressly eliminated the requirement for crimes against humanity to have a nexus with armed conflict. Furthermore, leading authorities such as Professor Lauterpacht, Professor Jennings, Professor Clark and, indeed, Professor Meron support the view that there is no requirement at the present time (and has not been a requirement for some substantial period of time) for any type of a nexus between crimes against humanity and armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So what do we do then with Article 5? It says "when committed in armed conflict, whether international or internal".

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: We pay attention to our Statute, your Honour. We are not suggesting anything other than that. The Statute imposes that requirement. It is our submission that the linkage is relatively loose and, essentially, means occurring while an armed conflict is on, but we are not suggesting in any way that the Statute should not be fully complied with. All we are suggesting is that it has been drafted a bit more narrowly than existing customary law would permit. For that reason, because it is narrower than is necessary, it clearly does not offend the nullum crimen principle.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we then have to find, if we get to that point, for allegations that are made under Article 5, we would have to find then that there was an armed conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but I do not think there would have to be a particularly tight linkage between the offence and the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just the existence. FENRICK: So, is there a conflict in Bosnia? Yes, there is. Okay, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then because it says "international or internal", we would have to find one or the other and the Defence says we would have to find that it is international.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: We dispute that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say that is not so because of the various Conventions, Genocide, Apartheid, etc..

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Have recognised the crimes against humanity may be committed in the absence of an armed conflict, but I suppose none have said: "Well, assuming an armed conflict exists, it need not be international, internal is enough"?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I am unaware of any that approach it in quite that way, your Honour, which is exactly the reason why we approached it the way we did. We do not want to argue that it was originally something for just international, and it has expanded to include armed conflict. From our point of view, from close to the point of origin of the concept, crimes against humanity has been viewed as something which is independent of armed conflict as a concept and as a part of current customary law. Because of that, the only relevance of that provision in Article 5 is it restricts what we could have done, perhaps, if we had been given unlimited jurisdiction over crimes against humanity but, nevertheless, it clearly does not offend in any way the nullum crimen principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Are you saying this then, that since learned writers in 1992 were saying that there was no requirement of armed conflict in the case of crimes against humanity, it must a fortiori be the case that there was no requirement of international conflict? If you did not need conflict at all, obviously you did not need an international one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is as simple as that, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, it is, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: If I might just sum up very briefly, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: The judges and lawyers who argued and decided war crimes cases in the aftermath of the Second World War were compelled to exercise a degree of creativity to fill in gaps in the law because the international humanitarian law of 1907 (the Hague Conventions) and 1929 (the Geneva Conventions) was not sufficiently comprehensive. The task before us now is somewhat similar because of the way in which international humanitarian law is compelled to develop. There is no international law equivalent to the domestic legislatives and judicial systems which engage in a continued process of developing national criminal law. International humanitarian law generally develops through treaties and the accretion of custom. The law which this Tribunal will apply must be the treaty and customary law of today, not the law of 1945. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does that conclude the Prosecutor's remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin has.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How long do you think your reply would take?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have to prepare anyhow, your Honour, and I think you will take time for lunch. So, if Mr. Vujin may address the court before you will adjourn and then if we may come back at half past 2?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That would be fine. I was going to determine whether, perhaps, we could break for lunch now but, Mr. Vujin, you wish to proceed now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the explanations that we heard this morning from Mr. Fenrick as an explanation of the Prosecutor to the motions that we made are, obviously, based on opinions that the Defence cannot accept and which are contrary to the views of the Defence. As regards our claims that the Security Council did not, legally speaking, have the authority to establish this Tribunal is also indicated by a book entitled "The New World Order and the Control of the legality of the Security Council Enactments" published by Mr. Mohammed Bedjawee, at that time President of the International Court of Justice in The Hague. In this Article he wonders whether the idea is ripe for exercising control supervision by some other body over the decisions of the Security Council. It is particularly interesting to note whether this right should be accorded to the International Court of Justice in The Hague as the main judiciary organ of the United Nations. So, it is evident that among lawyers also there are different views and different attitudes on this matter which give the Defence the feeling that they are right, that we have chosen the right path, that this path should also be legally regulated properly for all countries, all states, in the world. The part of the statement made in which they attempted to show that the Federal Republic Yugoslavia was in war in Bosnia is, obviously, based on a lack of knowledge of this problem or, rather, insufficient knowledge related to the disintegration of Yugoslavia, more precisely the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, its disintegration, and is also based on a certain confusion in the facts that are being used. My colleague, Simic, is going to add a few words from the constitutional side because he is an expert on constitutional matters, but I shall say only one thing, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic at the first elections he won in 1990, 879,260 votes from the voters that actually went to the polls, and that Mr. Fikret Abdic won 1,045,000 votes. According to the constitution of Bosnia and according to the rules and regulations governing these elections, Mr. Fikret Abdic was supposed to be the President of Bosnia Herzegovina. He did not become President. Rather, Alija Izetbegovic became President; a man who wanted to turn Bosnia into an Islamic state, an Islamic state in the middle of Europe. The Serbian sides was opposed to this, that is, the Serbs and also the Croats who live in Bosnia, but also Muslims who were opposed to Alija Izetbegovic and who were supporters of Fikret Abdic. Now the situation is the following: You know full well that Hercog Bosnia was proclaimed as a community. This was way back in 1991, on November 19th, in the town of Gruda. The community of Croats was proclaimed as Hercog Bosnia. And after that, on August 27th 1993, the Bosnian Croats proclaimed their own state. You also know that now you also have an autonomous province which was proclaimed which is headed by Mr. Fikret Abdic. Then also there is the Republic of Srpska, then you also have the Bosnian Muslim part under Alija Izetbegovic. That is the reality of Bosnia. Before that, there was Bosnia as a single state which, according to the constitution, consisted of all these nations, these peoples. They did not have the right to secede from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, according to the constitution of the SFRY. Therefore, the Army, the JNA, was present throughout the country because it was the constitutional right of the Army to defend the borders of the state. Through the one sided secession of Slovenia and Croatia that were, regrettably, sanctioned through the recognition of all other states (and they did become states) contrary to these provisions because the world hastened to recognise these states, this created a confusion and a feeling that now the Yugoslav Army is the common army of all these people who lived together under the idea of fraternity and unity, and now that all of a sudden this army turned into an occupation army. This is impossible anywhere in the world and this has been impossible and this is impossible. This Army consisted of conscripts of young people, young men, Croats, Serbs, Macedonians, Muslims, Bosnians. They were retreating and they were attacked both in Slovenia and Croatia and later in Bosnia also. They were retreating and they suffered casualties along the way because they did not defend themselves and they were not engaged in fighting. Only afterwards, when they were directly attacked, then there were certain counter acts, but this is not a conflict. They simply were trying to leave these territories where this Army was not welcome any longer because they were considered to be an alien armed force. I am saying time and again that this is a confusion and that, therefore, this Army had to retreat now, a part of this Army, because, for example, all the Croats who served in that Army, they would stay in Croatia. Also when the army was retreating from Bosnia, then the Muslims remained there with the weapons they had. They remained on that territory and after that they continued fighting the Serbs who remained there, because on 13th May 1992 the Republic of Srpska formed its army. I also wish to draw your attention to certain opinions which, clearly, confirm this thesis of the Defence because are things that cannot simply be overlooked. Sorry, just a minute. I am trying to find this in your papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You are putting this all, as I understand it, to the issue of it not being an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Sorry, for one minute. Sorry, this is a very important opinion given by Henry Kissinger; I must find it. I will find it in the meantime, but I just want to draw your attention to an interview given by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic to Speigel in July 1991 where he says: "There will centrally be a civil war which will be impossible to bring to an end". After civil war, civil war is what is at stake. It is a civil war.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You take your time; I am curious as to what Henry Kissinger said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Sorry, just a moment, yes. The former Secretary of State of the United States, Henry Kissinger, wrote an Article that he published in the Los Angeles Times on 16th May 1993: "It is important to realise that Bosnia has never been a separate nation and that there is no distinct Bosnian cultural identity. There must (... reading to the words...) of the current tragedy of international recognition of a Bosnian State Government by Muslims blindly following the President of Germany's hasty recognition of Slovenia and Croatia, but whereas as Croatia and Slovenia had their own identity, Bosnia was (... reading to the words...) It is mystery how anyone could even think that Croats and Serbs are willing to stay together in the ... Yugoslavia, could be induced to create a joint state in Bosnia together with Muslims they hated for centuries". Mr. Kissinger kept advocating the point, which is the right point of view, that in Bosnia there is a civil and religious war that is going on. It is a civil war, and I go back to that because now, in reality, we have four groups that are practically fighting against each other more or less, namely, the Croats in Hercog Bosnia, then the Muslims supporting Fikret Abdic in Western Bosnia, then there is the Republic of Srpska and the Muslims under Alija Izetbegovic who has only one small part of the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that is what we have. We have here many statements made by various people such as Mr. Christopher who said on 17th June 1993: "Premature recognisation of Croatia and Bosnia and ... caused the civil war" -- all of them speaking about civil war. Therefore, the standpoint of the Prosecution that this is an international conflict, especially a conflict in which the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would take part, is out of place and it is not based on actual facts. I do not want to keep you much longer. My colleague Mr. Simic is going to say a few words about the constitutional aspect about the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have a lot of problems in terms of compiling evidence. Among other things, because our legal systems differ considerably, that is to say, the legal system of the former Yugoslavia and the legal system upon which the work of this Tribunal is based. Therefore, I request you kindly that these objections that we have raised, and that the Prosecution now believes that we should prove what we are saying, kindly give us a certain period of time and we are going to substantiate everything that I have told you about. We are going to give you all these statements and all this proof, this evidence, these opinions and also professional papers in this field. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have just one question, Mr. Vujin, regarding your request for time. By what standard, what level of proof, I suppose -- I address it really to all the parties; I just kind of thought about it -- must we find that an international conflict existed? There has been some discussion as to whether or not that is one of the elements of the crime that an international conflict existed or is it not. Certainly, if it were one of the elements of the crime, then the Prosecutor would have to establish that it is beyond a reasonable doubt, which no decision has been made on this. So that would be a very high finding, I guess. Now, though, this issue has been presented to us in a jurisdictional posture, the filing of a motion challenging jurisdiction. Obviously, we do not need to find that an international conflict existed, if we need to find it, beyond a reasonable doubt. The reason that just occurred to me, Mr. Vujin, is that you said: "Give us time to explain about this conflict". I was wondering whether you are suggesting that if we proceed to trial that you would put on more evidence about this. So does everyone understand the question, I guess certainly not beyond a reasonable doubt. Mr. Vujin, do you have any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No. You did not understand me properly. What I have been saying is that, just as the Prosecution believes that these are public documents, that we do not have to give the court something that is a public document. We thought that what we have pointed out was sufficient for you to decide as a court on the jurisdiction of this court based on our motions, but the Prosecution keeps repeating: "You have to prove; you have to prove; you have to prove". To prove our standpoint by somebody else's opinion is something that is inconceivable to us. We have a whole lot of such opinions published all over the world and in our country too, and we believe that since this was public knowledge that we did not have to bring this forth. Also, the Prosecution says that the constitution of the Republic of Srpska says that they are part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that that has proved that this is an international conflict. For example, if the Netherlands or if anybody else said in their constitution: "We are part of Canada; we are an integral part of the United States of America", would they really be part of the United States of America or Canada, if this is not what the constitution of Canada or the USA would say. And no such thing exists in the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There are many such examples. I have just mentioned this one in passing. So, of course, I hope this will have no repercussions on your decision and on the further discussion that we will have.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do I understand, Mr. Simic, that you need to speak before the lunch break?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: 10 minutes, yes

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will not be available after our lunch recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I shall speak very briefly. I could speak after lunch, though.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you will be here then, why do we not stand in recess until 2.30? (Luncheon adjournment) .

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will hear from Mr. Simic at this point. Mr. Simic, try again and make sure Mr. Tadic is hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Translation commences at this point): ... is the constitution solution that was made in the Former Yugoslavia. It is precisely from these routes that we today are in a very serious war and many nations suffer from this. Bosnia-Herzegovina used to be a Federal unit in the Former Yugoslavia. The first constitution was passed in 1946 whereby it was stipulated that it would be a country of six states, but based on the principle of the unification of the singularity of people and these peoples that made Yugoslavia were Slovenia, Croatia, the Slovenes, the Croats, the Serbs, the Montenegroes and Macedonians. At that time the Muslims were not a people, not a nationality. Although there were six republics, it was a community of five people and you have the armours of the Federal, Social Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with five symbols that represented five people; five torches represented five nationalities that formed one start. Later on with the evolution of the society there were several changes that were made. As Mr. Vujin said, the Muslims were a religious community which had all the rights, including the right of carrying out their religious habits, but they were not a nationality. According to the census at that time, they had the possibility to be determined as Serb Croats or to the category of "undetermined". Most of the Muslims at that time were either as their origins Croats or Serbs, depending on the territories they used to live in. I have to make a digression here. Mr. Izetbegovic at one of these censors could declare himself as being a Serb, but by the constitution of 174 the Muslims have become a nationality. It was a source of numerous debates whether they fulfilled all the requirements in order to become a nationality as determined by sociologists, but I will not go into the details here starting from the start. If they perceive themselves as being a category apart, then I cannot contest it. If they had the feeling to be a nationality, that is their right to develop their traditions in that way. But, on one condition, they cannot endanger others, other nationalities, that existed in the former Yugoslavia. There were two constitutions in the former Yugoslavia. There was the Federal constitution and the constitution of each Federal unit, but always the constitution of the Federal unit had to be in complete accordance with the Federal constitution. In the new constitution of 1974 Bosnia and Herzegovina is treated as a state of three, equally free, state making people, nationalities, which is the Serbs, Croats and Muslims having equal rights. It is precisely at that moment that some problems started to appear because the constitution of Yugoslavia that used to be a state of five nationalities has become a state with six nationalities, and on the armours of the Federal Republic a sixth torch had been added. But over then some aspirations appeared that Yugoslavia has to be divided by states, each nationality having its own state, the Serbs having Serbia, Macedonians Macedonia and so on. Here I can with full responsibility claim that the Bosnian tragedy starts at that particular moment, because the Bosnian Muslims used to be a religious community. They start to look at Bosnia as their own state. They create the Bosnian language which endangers the language of the Serbs and the Croats that had been used by everybody before. Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the place that divides the catholic community from the orthodox community, is the place where the Catholicism and orthodoxy intertwine. There were differences even in the language, but now with the arrival of Muslims, the question is, whose country is it? A state of Muslims or Serbs and Croats? But I have to say that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina had been a majority up until 1980 census. Before the Second World War, the last census shown from 1931 that the Serbs were a large majority. In the Second World War, Yugoslavia was with the allies and its nationalities have been victims of the Second World War. In the first place, the Serbs, because of some historic reasons, in the first period, Croatia became the ally of Hitler, Germany, and they proclaimed an independent state in which Bosnia-Herzegovina was included. At that time an horrendous genocide on Serbs was performed, and it is precisely in that region that the indictment is against Mr. Tadic. I think that precisely the emotions were so highly strung in these particular regions because of these historical reasons that have never been clearly stated. Trying to reinforce the Muslim nationality and trying to oust out the Serbs, in the statistics since 1961 up until 1981 in two censuses, out of Bosnia 385,000 Serbs left. After that, Muslims have become the majority, but not in absolute sense because before this last war there were about 43 per cent of the Muslim population in Bosnia. After the genocide in the Second World War and later on when the Serbs left, but in all other periods, the Serbs were the majority in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the moment when communism and socialism started to fade, the problems appeared in Yugoslavia. The process of democracy did not go into the direction of transforming the power and the principles. There were lots of national movements that appeared probably because of certain pressures that existed under communism where the national feelings could not be fully expressed and people were often persecuted because of their national feelings. The nationalities of the former Yugoslavia had gathered around the idea of the nation that should have been the solution of all our problems. In such a context the first elections are organised. Certain changes have come about in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Three national parties were founded as the (a) the Muslim nationality, HDZ of the Croatian population and SDS, the party of the Serbs. These were all national parties. The fact itself that those parties were founded on the national principle showed to all serious analysts that Bosnia-Herzegovina was heading towards a civil war unless a situation for the former Yugoslavia is found. In the election campaigns ------

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: When you say these were parties founded on a national basis, do you mean throughout the whole of Yugoslavia or do you mean having regard to whether they were -- you cannot hear -- when you say that the three parties were formed on a national basis, do you mean having regard to the nationality or do you mean throughout the whole of Yugoslavia when you say "founded on a national basis"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: It concerns the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina where three nationalities lived. These nationalities have determined themselves and chosen according to their national basis. There was not almost hardly a Serb in the SDA party or a Muslim in the SDS party. This principle of division was going towards a confrontation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are having some difficulty (and we going to resolve this after today) when you speak in your language it is translated, when you are speaking in your language, I think Mr. Tadic is listening on one channel, but then when Judge Stephens speaks in English, it is then translated and Mr. Tadic needs to know that he needs to switch to a different channel. The guards are helping him, but it sometimes takes a little while.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: When we speak in the language of the accused, he can hear without it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, and he did not originally put on his microphones, but I thought you told him to put on his microphones, so he can put on his microphones but just continue to listen in your language and then when you speak, though, it is going to have to be translated into a different channel, so sometimes if I am kind of waving at you, Mr. Simic, it is not to say "hello"; it is just to tell you that there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I caused it by interrupting you. You have explained. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, awaiting these problems, some changes have been made in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to avoid the conflict. One of the solutions that were passed through the constitutional amendments in 1990 was to create a Council for National Equality. The Council for National Equality would be an organ of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina with 20 deputies, 20 members from the three national parties, and all the decisions could be on the basis of the absolute unanimity in order to avoid preference from one nationality to the other in order not to endanger a particular nationality. But, unfortunately, through the strategy of the Muslim party that wanted Bosnia for itself, that Council was never properly founded or never ever had a single session, because the constitution even had such a provision that there would be a particular mechanism that would regulate their functioning of this council. In the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990, there is no possibility, no provision, that says that Bosnia-Herzegovina could secede from the former Yugoslavia. There was a provision concerning the changes of the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina that said that such changes could not be made without referendum in which all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina would take place. That is why it was after two-thirds, that is, 66 points of the electorate should vote in favour of such a change, but it only concerned the changes of the Republican borders inside Yugoslavia, and the Muslim leadership seized that occasion and after the elections in a very deft way, diplomatic way, they managed to turn the situation into their advantage. When the new Bosnian authorities were constituted that were supposed to represent the thee partners, SDA, HDZ and SDS, the actual power was divided in the following way. Mr. Izetbegovic was a President. Mr. Vujin said something about Mr. Abdic, a Muslim, who really won. The Vice President was Aubganic, also a Muslim, one of the most extremist representatives of SDA. The Prime Minister was Mr. Mline, who was a Croat. The Minister of Foreign Affairs was a Muslim, Mr. Salidic. The Secretary for the Police Department was another Muslim, Mr. Musavic. The Minister for Defence was Mr. Docker who was a Croat. The Governor of the Central Bank was a Muslim. So at the moment when the Serbs are accused of entering the war, the Muslim and partly to Croats, gained all the important positions.
