So if the Serbs really wanted to start into a civil war, or whatever you called it, conflict, how could they have let all the other partners have all the positions? Your Honour, I live in that country, and the essential question, was the relationship of Serbs towards Yugoslavia? The Serbs accepted everything because they counted on the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain part of Yugoslavia, and that that would not endanger all their rights, cultural and civil rights and religious rights, because Yugoslavia did exist and it functioned in one way or the other, because it was some kind of a roof that protected all the nationalities in that country. When the truce was lifted all the countries were exposed to various winds of history, of historic aspirations, so all these fears were justified. It was very difficult to become a national minority. Everybody was afraid of that. These fears appeared in the population. How much it was certain that this war would appear is very well illustrated by Millivan Dillus who was a dissident and who spends many years fighting for democracy in Yugoslav jails. On the Sarajevo television he said, just before the elections: "If there will be no Yugoslavia, there will be no Bosnia-Herzegovina". That was the mere truth and one should have taken it into account. It was a complete Utopia to discuss in which way Bosnia and Herzegovina would maintain itself because we called them "a small Yugoslavia". When larger and better organised Yugoslavia broke up, it was a complete utopia to expect it to last. It is very difficult for you to understand, and it sometimes seems so very awkward to hear some specialists from New York, for example, explain certain things as experts when four years ago they did not really know where Bosnia was. After the war in Croatia, since 1992, there were enormous fears there, enormous incidents. The incidents were happening on a daily basis. On 2nd of March 1992 in Sarajevo, the very centre, the Muslim extremists shoot on a Serbian wedding party only because the Serbs had a Serb flag with them. People were killed. The bridegroom's father, then the Serbian orthodox priest was severely wounded. After that the problems appear in Sarajevo. There was a rising. The first barricades appeared, but if somebody would like to try to study, there were quite a few occasions and quite a few events like that on the territory of the whole of Bosnia Herzegovina but, nevertheless, the Muslim leaderships decides to go on a referendum to proclaim an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, apart from all the requirements made by the Serbian party who ask all the questions to be resolved at the Council for National Equality. At that session of Parliament that lasted for about two days, the Serbs were asking for other things, but the decision was to go at the referendum. The referendum took place between 29th February and 1st March 1992. The Serbs did not want to take part in the referendum. The Croats did take part in it, but it was a purely tactical matter because the Croats, even before the Serbs had proclaimed their Hercog Bosnia, which stills functions in that area and which today has got its local authorities, its structure of power, and I can assert today that since Hercog Bosnia appeared, never ever a single currency had entered from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I know that it was not the case in the Serbian Republic. Nevertheless, the Croats had to enter on the referendum for tactical reasons because otherwise they would have stayed in Yugoslavia which would have been a catastrophe from their national point of view. But that was only against the constitution because the constitutional provisions said something only about the internal borders within Yugoslavia, but even like that, it did not give the right to the Bosnian Muslims and Croats to proclaim an independent state. I already told you that 66 per cent of the electorate had to vote for it, but the official results of the referendum say that only 62 per cent of the electorate voted "yes" at the referendum. That means that there was no possibility to proclaim independence. But the leadership of the Mr. Izetbegovic led by Mr. Izetbegovic's idea which -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Sorry, if we are going to follow you, I have to interrupt you. I have a statement here which says that 63 per cent of eligible voters participated in the vote and over 90 per cent of those who voted for independence. Are you saying those figures are wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The data that you give are probably correct but, according to the constitution, out of the complete eligible voters, 66 per cent have to vote in favour, 90 per cent of Muslims, Croats, participated and between 62 and 63 per cent were there. So 66 of eligible voters were not present because the Serbs did not participate. With such a situation, many incidents occurred, and the situation was very tense, especially regarding the JNA, especially because JNA, the Yugoslav National Army, is extremely important element of all these events. That is why I will have to give some additional information. The JNA was the army of all the nationalities or all the states, if you allow me that expression. The professional soldiers, the officers, and also as the recruits from the conscription were the young men of a certain age had to do the military service. This was valid for all the nationalities, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Slovenes. The Army had also property, the systems, barracks, airports. The Army had also the military industry. The JNA counted on the fact that Yugoslavia would be an eternal state. All the military equipment and industry were situated in the centre of Yugoslavia in Bosnia in order that the enemy could not reach them. Nowadays, 70 per cent of the JNA made by the former Yugoslavia is on the territory controlled by Muslim and Croats, like Travnik, Vtus, Gorazde and Sarajevo. Amongst the officers, they tried to follow the percentage of nationalities in order to have a certain percentage among the officers, the commanding staff, that would represent all the nationalities. It used to be one state. Mr. Vukranyans who was the Commander of the Sarajevo army district, he used to live in Sarajevo. He was from Ujistza, but he had been living at that time for 10 years in Sarajevo. His family lived there. His children went to school there. Then the war starts. The Army is proclaimed to be an occupational army which is, from the legal point of view, something that cannot be maintained. So there are problems with officers. Many incidents occurred. After the declaration of independence made by Bosnia and Herzegovina and, especially, I think, that happened on 7th April 1992 when the European Union recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina, the problem starts to be dealt with. The problems that appear between the JNA and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that direction an agreement was made about the withdrawal of the JNA out of Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to that agreement, JNA should withdraw up to 19th May. Why 19th May? Because the Army, with all its people and equipment and so on, it is not a husband who leaves his wife, just taking his toothbrush with him. The Army had to leave -- until 19th May the Army did obey by that agreement and left Bosnia and Herzegovina until 19th May, from which it appears that the thesis made by the Prosecution that the Army was an occupation army until 19th May is something that cannot be maintained. How an occupational army? How could they have arrived there? Because in that Army was made of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats, Serbs and Muslims. What happened to the property of the JNA? According to the Commander, the property belonged to that party. If the Commander of a particular barracks was a Muslim, the property went to the Muslims. If it was a Bosnian Serb, they made it, and at the same time a lot of its property was simply taken away. Something happened in the street called the (indecipherable) Street in Sarajevo when the barracks were going out -- the militaries were going out of the barracks. Many problems happened. Mr. Garnic led the operation of putting fire on 40 young men in order to pull the Army out of Sarajevo. So, there is no foundation that could lead us to a certain fact that the JNA at any single moment in Bosnia and Herzegovina had any element of a foreign military force because, according to the agreement, it left Bosnia and Herzegovina on 19th May. Both these questions, I reaffirm, are set in the context that in Bosnia and Herzegovina the conflict is one of a civil war, and all the consequences that can be attached to it can in order -- if that message could get to the foreign mediators and all the parties, the conflict will end much sooner because it is really a civil war and a religious war. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, we do not have any questions, Mr. Simic, at this time. I imagine we will have to determine what evidentiary value to be given to your statement. I appreciate what you have said. I have heard you and I have heard Mr. Fenrick. I am sure we will hear more if we proceed to trial. Thank you very much. Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have any additional arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you, your Honour. The Defence agrees with the Prosecution that the trial of Tadic can only take place if the trial is to be fair. There is no doubt about it. This requirement, however, does not amount to the argument raised by the Defence yesterday. What we argued yesterday was, just in brief, that the Tribunal was competent to subject the establishment of the Tribunal to a limited judicial review. Limited, that is, to say whether the decision taken by the Security Council was consistent with previous action taken by the Council since the competence to establish the Tribunal is not expresis verbis in the Charter. The competence to do so, to review within this limitation, just marginal review, the competence to do so, derives from the human right of Mr. Tadic to be tried by a court established by law. The difference between the point of view of the Prosecution and the position we have taken is that the review should include the establishment of the Tribunal -- let me start it again. I think I will phrase it in a different way. The Defence differs from the Prosecution, however, in stating that the review should include the establishment of the Tribunal and should not be limited to the proceedings before your court. We must admit, however, that we have not fully understood what sort of review the Prosecution has in mind, because it seems to us that when you ask questions about this issue that some kind of marginal review is also in the mind of the Prosecution. So we are not sure whether, at the end of the day, there is some difference between the Defence and the Prosecution. But we take the position that reviewing within the margins as we have laid down it implies that "review" means including the review of the establishment and not only reviewing in the context of a fair trial only related to the proceedings. As argued and argued yesterday, the decision of the Security Council to establish the Tribunal was, in fact, arbitrary and capricious, if there is any relevant distinction between these words. It seems that, in our mind, there is no difference; it is one and the same notion but maybe the Prosecution may elaborate this distinction. Moreover, the arbitrariness and the capriciousness may arise during the proceeding. For example, if the Prosecutor was to decide that it would only prosecute people with grey hair, it had nothing to do with the establishment, but then we move to the proceedings itself. Such a decision would not be open for review by your Tribunal since the Statute does not provide for such a review. So, even if you look into the problem in this respect, one may wonder, what is a fair trial in this? As far as we have understood the Prosecution, it follows from their position that even if the Prosecution were to be arbitrary and capricious in nature, as long as the trial itself remains fair, everything is fine. We cannot accept that. In the Defence's view, the treaty on the law of treaties, the Treaty of Vienna, does not preclude an extensive interpretation resulting in a "reparation" of obvious shortcomings of the Statute to meet the demands of a fair trial. So we feel that you will have to exercise your powers under the Statute with an extensive interpretation in order to meet in full conformance with the fair trial notion as we have argued yesterday. Apparently, we do differ fundamentally in our interpretation of the relevant provisions of the UN Charter concerning the powers of the Security Council. At this moment, it seems quite pointless to ask to repeat everything we have argued yesterday. I may, therefore, just refer to the transcript. We have discussed the matter yesterday quite extensively. What we have heard today, at least in the opinion of the Defence, does not view anything new and, therefore, we might refer, indeed, to the transcript. That brings me to Mr. Fenrick. From here I have taken my notes in Dutch, so I will have to translate it while I speak. I hope you will forgive me if I do it quite slowly. The first question which has been raised after listening to Mr. Fenrick is, it did not become clear in his presentation, what now are the new facts of new evidence that might lead to a different view of the matter since December 1992, because it seems to the Defence that all the elements he has discussed today are the same elements which have been viewed when writing this comment at the end of December 1992. So we are not convinced that there is a new basis for a new view, but rather a change of view on the same elements. The second observation I want to make is that, as far as we discussed about the period ending on May 19th 1992, it seems not pointful or, I had better say, it seems pointless to discuss all the elements that might lead to an internal or an international armed conflict, because we agree that before that time, starting from the date of independence of the Bosnian Republic, the Muslim Republic, we do agree that there was an international armed conflict going on. So it does not make much sense to dispute that matter, though listening to Mr. Simic there is some nuance in it, as you may have noticed. The whole issue relates to what happened after the 19th. What I have tried to argue yesterday is a quite different position than has been taken today by the Prosecution. I mean, the essence of our different positions is that we have argued that you should limit the scope of your assessment on the issue of whether it be an international or an internal conflict, it should be limited to the area and should be limited in time. What I have heard from Mr. Fenrick's presentation, it seems to us that there is no objection in limitation in time, though the limitation in area has only been disputed. I have nothing to add to what I have said yesterday about the reasons why it would be very reasonable to limit your scope of assessment to the area and not to take into account the whole area of Bosnia, so also in this sense it seems quite pointless to repeat all this. There is some inconsistency, as it seems to us, when the Prosecution is arguing that, whereas the Bosnian Serbs have declared themselves independent by that declaration, they also noted in their constitution that citizens of their own Republic are also having the Yugoslavian, nationality and for that reason the conflict between the Bosnian Serbs and the Muslim government should be viewed as an international conflict for that reason. We do not accept that argument but, even accepting that, it would mean that you cannot argue in the same time that by the independence of Bosnia you will have to take into account the whole territory. So we feel that if you will accept the first argument, then as a logical consequence of it you will also have to accept that you will have the scope of a limited area and not the whole territory of Bosnia, because that is not consistent with the position that the Bosnian Serbs have also a double nationality. It seems to us that the Prosecutor is having the best of both worlds. You cannot; we all know. You will have to choose. Then in the presentation of the Prosecution, we missed any example of any action of the Yugoslav National Army, that is, the undivided Army up to May 19th. We missed any example of any action of that Army after May 19th 1992. The only thing we have seen in this matter is in the document which has been presented by the Prosecution to your court. That relates only to equipment leaving on the spot equipment, leaving on the spot the barracks, leaving on the spot weapons, but not the delivery of weapons after that date or any action by the Army by itself after that date. So here we have a problem in what are the fact we are discussing today.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, may I ask you one question? I want to just understand your position. Prior to May 19th 1992, if the JNA was in the Prijedor region, would the grave breaches be applicable to that region?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In our view not, because there was not a conflict going on, but even if -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why was there not a conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You mean there was no-one fighting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That occurred later.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: After May 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No fighting in Prijedor before May 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In the area of the place where all the events happened in the Opstina of Prijedor, Prijedor itself was taken over on April 30th. That is also in the report of Professor Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: April 13th?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 30th. By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: By the Serbs, not by armed force. It was politically taken over.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But not with the assistance of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There was not an army fighting at that place. The place was not shut, was not destroyed by any violence or armed conflict, being it an army... There was no army there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When did the JNA then come into the Opstina of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the JNA never was there. The JNA has never been in the Opstina of Prijedor. Let us put this exactly: Before 19th May, the JNA was in the area in the barracks, been there all the tile since 1980, since 1970.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But engaged in no conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But not engaged in a conflict because the taking over of Prijedor itself, the town, on April 30th 1992 was not through means of weapons. It was a political takeover, and later after the 19th, then armed forces of the Serb Government came in conflict with the villages of Gozaric and others and those were not taken over by political means but by means of arms.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Serbs were taking that over between 30th April through May 19th then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, no after the 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What happened between April 30th and May 19th -- nothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There were no armed conflicts going on and on 30th April also no armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So when was there armed conflict, if ever, in your view, in the Opstina of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It started in the morning of 24th.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. After that the JNA had left their barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, before.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: On 19th they left the barracks and the armoury and all the other things to the local Commander. He took it over as an Officer of the Serb Bosnian Republic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that on May 19th or before?.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: On 19th, as far as I am informed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, the JNA left their equipment but if the lieutenant in charge or the captain in charge was a Serb, he went home, is that what you are saying, to Yugoslavia or no, he stayed there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Several of them left. The main part stayed but had a new employer.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You know, we cannot all talk at the same time, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, some left, some stayed. Those who left were Yugoslavs not choosing to be a Bosnian Serb. They were not of Serb/Bosnian descent, so they left. Those who stayed in the barracks were those who were born there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And took control at least of a portion of the ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- the material that formally belonged to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As happened everywhere in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand. Some went to Croats, some went to others, but in any case after that time then there was an army that was controlled by the Bosnian Serbs ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- using material left from the former Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. That is what happened everywhere in Bosnia. Those under command of the Muslims had those armoury; those under the control of the Bosnian Croats, those in the control of the Bosnian Serbs. Then the armed conflict occurred on certain spots and, as we talk about the Opstina of Prijedor, on 24th it started in Kavadic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So it is your position that an international armed conflict never occurred in that region, in the Opstina of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I confine myself to the period after 19th and then I say, no, there was no international armed conflict. Before, there was not a conflict at all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There was no international armed conflict after May 19th 1992 and no armed conflict in that area before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Given your description of the division of material, has there been an international armed conflict in any portion of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There has?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Because at those places there was an engagement of armed forces of JNA before 19th and armed forces under the control of the Muslim government.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of the who?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Muslim government.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then whenever there is a conflict between the JNA, under the control of the JNA, as opposed to when they divided, their material -----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Under the control of Belgrade, on the central control of Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then there would be an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If that occurred, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, from your point of view, the test is to look, to determine whether or not the JNA at a particular time was under the direct control of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Only if that is found will there be an international armed conflict anywhere in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is a different question, because you have understood what we discussed yesterday, that we limit it to the area of Prijedor. We dispute that looking into the problem should take also into account any other part of former Yugoslavia, because if you do so, you would also accept that Danish people from German descent, living on the island of Jutland, taking over from the neighbours would impose a national conflict on the Jutland.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will see what the Security Council would do in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But that is not the point; the point is what you will do in that situation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I know, but in this instance -- so what you are saying is at least in that area the JNA was never under the control of Belgrade when there was an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What impact, if at all, does the involvement of Croatia in that area have to do with our determination of whether or not there was ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, because there was no involvement of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So in other areas, though, which we may have to resolve, that may be another ingredient but we do not have to deal with it in this area if we accept your argument that we should look at a particular geographical area, just the Opstina of Prijedor, and no international conflict because there was never a conflict with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It was in the heart of the Bosnian/Serbian Republic and the conflict occurred on the borders.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not within the region, though, Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But certainly not in the region. If we limit our scope in time, then the answer is very easy. There was not such a conflict whatsoever with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The scope of the indictment is May to August, some date in May and some date to August; between this period of time no armed conflict with the JNA controlled by Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And that should be our test?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is the test. That brings me to the Articles of the Statute itself. As a matter of fact, we discussed Article 2, did we not? The alternative of the applicability of the grave breaches provision of Article 2 and 147 of the Geneva Convention IV is that parties had an agreement under Article 3 of the Geneva Convention IV. The Prosecution has taken the position that that may be shown by the agreement of 22nd May and the agreement of 27th August. To start with, the agreement of 22nd May, we have argued that there is no direct reference to the grave breaches provisions. If we look into the agreement, it is not without sense, as we feel, that only particular articles of the Geneva Convention IV has been referred to, and explicitly not Article 147. Then the Prosecution maintains that we could understand from Article 5 of this agreement that the grave breaches might be in it. But if we read it (and you may read it yourselves), there is no reference to any grave breach. It is just a general reference of maintaining the Convention and not to offend, and if offences, without any reference to grave breaches, it says that offences should be prosecuted, and that is it. So it leaves the question completely open and, therefore, we dispute that this May agreement could be a basis for the applicability of the grave breaches provision. The unilateral declaration of August 27th, we feel that although it might be a reference, we disputed that, but even if we accept that there is some reference in it to establish an application of the grave breaches provisions of the Geneva Convention IV, in the same time the Prosecution has not solved the problem that this unilateral statement was made on August 27th, and that is after the period of the offence that has occurred and has been charged to Mr. Tadic. It seems to us that the question is totally irrelevant. Then the argument was that, why to agree on the exchange of prisoners with reference to the grave breaches, and would that not be a finger pointing that Article, the grave breaches provision, was after all included in the agreement of May 22nd? Also, here we feel that the Prosecution wants the best of both worlds because this same argument does not apply to the unilateral declarations of August 27th. Then the Prosecutor says: "Well, just in reaffirment". That seems very inconsistent, in our view.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, I do not know a lot about contract law, but if a contract is vague can you use subsequent statements made by parties to you to explain the meaning of a contract? I guess there are books on there. We can go and look.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sure, I am not going to elaborate the problem, but it seems to me that if the other statements are relevant to understand the previous agreement, yes, you may use them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So what I am saying is if there was an agreement on May 22nd 1992, then their unilateral statements, August 27th 1992 -- and, you are right; that is a little late -- can August 27th 1992 unilateral declarations be used to explain an ambiguous or vague contract if one existed on May 22nd?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What would be the sense of reading the agreement of 27th of August as a reaffirment if it explicitly says that the grave breaches are in it, as is maintained by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are right. That is what they say. But 147 is not in there. They want us to look at agreements 5 or point 5 to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But it is not in point 5 either.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand your argument regarding that, but let us suppose we say it is not explicit there, but this subsequent statement sheds light on their intentions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We take the position that, whereas in the unilateral agreement of 27th August the reference was more explicit than in the agreement of 22nd May, and whereas in the Exchange of the Prisoners Agreement it is explicit, we cannot understand that from this it is argued that although it is not explicit in the agreement of 22, they meant it to be explicit. We feel that if it was meant explicit, as it might be on 27th August, and it was certainly in the Prisoners Exchange Agreement, they should have done it also on 22nd May. There is no reason to believe that they did not mean it. It was argued in that time, if we do recall the context of what happened on 22nd May, there is no doubt that the issue of grave breaches was on the table. So it is not to be understood that it was not in the agreement if people wishes to have it in the agreement, so we do not accept that you just read it in. That brings me to Article 3 of the Statute. We have maintained the position that a common Article 3 is not included in Article 3 of the Statute. Before going into that, I think I might first give you an answer on the American amicus curiae letter before you remember me, I will do that by myself. Let me just read it because it is quite complicated. It says that the United States believe that the grave breaches provision of Article 2 of the Tribunal also apply to armed conflicts of a non-international character as well as those of an international character. That idea is based on Article No. 30 of the Geneva Convention III. It is, indeed, a novelty and it is a novelty, therefore, if we read the wording of Article No. 30. It says that, "Grave breaches to which the preceding Article relates shall be those involving any of the following acts if committed" -- this is important -- "against persons or property protected by the Convention". It seems that the government of the United States is arguing that "by the Convention", the words "by the Convention", should be read as not in the context of this Convention, but it should be read as applying to all the Geneva Conventions and, therefore, also to Convention IV. We feel that you cannot read this in the wording of this Article because otherwise it would have read "protected by the Conventions", an "s" after the "n". But there are more arguments to it. The context of the Geneva Convention III is, of course, a quite different context than the context of the Geneva Convention IV. So by just simply supposing that any offence committed against persons or property would constitute a violation of each of the Conventions and, more specifically, the Convention No. IV, is not based on any argument we can find in the Convention itself because the Conventions are separate. Each Convention regulates its own subject, and you cannot just interchange the subject of one Convention into the other. That is exactly what in this amicus curiae brief has been done. Thirdly, if we suppose that the drafters of the Statute would like to have the grave breaches provision in Article 2 of the Statute also be included for armed conflicts of a non-international character, why then would the drafter of the Statute not have written, as has been in Article 5, whether it be international or internal in character? They did not. The last argument is you may find that in Article 130 of Geneva III the word "by the Convention" could refer to the other Conventions. An argument for that idea might be that in Article 147 of the Geneva Convention IV the same phrase reads "against persons or property protected by the present Convention". Then, I would say, that this possibility is blocked by the wording in Article 2 of the Statute that reads "under the provisions of the relevant Geneva Convention". For that reason, we believe that for these four reasons it is, indeed, a novelty not to be followed by your Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is it then ingenuous, perhaps not altogether frank, for the amicus brief to say: "For example, Article 130"? That is not just one of a number of examples that might be quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have not read any other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is the only case, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I have read all the other ones. 3 is the only one that might be ambiguous on the wording, but is at the end of the day not. Speaking about the amicus curiae brief, I might say that the Defence was not quite amused by reading the last sentence of this brief. I think it is not appropriate in the spirit of Rule 74 of the Rules. The spirit of an amicus curiae brief is to learn the Tribunal about law, but not to take any position. We regret that the government of the United States has taken any position in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Every amicus brief that we have received has taken a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Up to now I have not read any one that ends with a conclusion advising you on taking a position. It is a learned letter that helps us to understand the law. It is the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We had our in camera on the motion for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It did not conclude in such a way. Read them again. That was just a personal remark. Article 3 of the Statute, we maintained the position that common Article 3 of the Geneva Convention is not included in Article 3. We have maintained the position that Article 3 of the Statute clearly refers to the words of The Hague Convention. We feel that the offences as listed up to (e) of Article 3 of the Statute is also an indication that it does refer to The Hague Conventions and there is no indication that it could also refer to any other Convention. So for that reason we do not accept that, frankly, we could read any other kind of offence within the framework of this Article. The question whether you could raise such a reading from the Nicaragua case will be explained by Mr. Orie, so I will leave that aside. We have not yet given you any authority for our position that we feel that common Article 3 is not a part of Article 3 of the Statute because we have argued yesterday we have not found any authority that it is. We give you one authority that it is not. That is the authority of Professor van Kalshoven who was the President of the Committee of Experts. During a conference on the International Criminal Court for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague on February 16th 1995 he made the following statement. I will read that statement to you: "Inspiration for this text", and we are then talking about Article 3 of the Statute "and, in effect, its very rather dated wording, comes from a much older treaty, the 1907 The Hague Convention, respecting the laws and customs of war on land, to be more precise, from the annexed regulations on the self-same laws and the customs of land warfare. While the origin of the regulations may be tracked back to the instructions President Lincoln issued in 1863 to the Northern troops in the American Civil War, the Convention regulations of 1907 were assigned to cover no other situations than 'war'. That is an armed conflict between states. They were neither written nor intended for situations of internal armed conflicts. Here again, therefore, the competence of Tribunal appears to go no further than to deal with violations of law and customs of war committed in situations of international armed conflict. In effect, it is very doubtful indeed that there will exist such a thing as the The Hague 'laws and customs' of internal armed conflict in a more general sense." End of statement. It seems to us that in the framework of this statement we feel that, also in the opinion of the Professor, there is no precedent for the idea that common Article 3 is well-established international law leading to the effect that it is a part of Article 3 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have a citation to that or did you provide that with your attachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I did not, but I will.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. That brings me to Article 5 and that Article will also be covered by Mr. Orie, so these were remarks I had in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will just make a few short remarks in addition to what Mr. Wladimiroff has said until now. The first remark concerns the interpretation of the jurisdiction granted in Article 5. It has been argued by the Prosecutor that the Statute gives a far more restrictive provision on the extent of the jurisdiction, because it states "in an armed conflict" than would have been possible under customary international law. As a matter of fact, I fail to see the relevance of the remarks made on this issue, because under customary international law there is hardly any restriction -- I would not say no restriction; I may refer to the Lotus case -- to the assumption of jurisdiction by states. But this wide discretion to assume jurisdiction does not mean that there is jurisdiction just because there is a wide discretion to assume it. It is the legislature, the domestic legislature, which will have to do it, otherwise there is no jurisdiction. I must say when I am talking about legislative organs, I get a bit confused these days because until now I heard that the Security Council is not just an executive organ, it is also, as I heard this morning, a legislative organ and this legislative organ is passing adjudicative powers which it might not have to this Tribunal. So I must say from a point of view of what I learned to be constitutional law, I get a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Omnipotent, it appears; what you are saying is they are claiming all these powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: They are claiming -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Executive legislative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I wanted to say. I will just give you an example on this problem of assuming jurisdiction: If we look at customary international law, there is no problem whatsoever in assuming jurisdiction on the basis of the nationality of the offender. On the other hand, we see that, especially under Anglo American law, that -- I am not talking about antitrust law, but in general criminal law -- the states limit themselves in assuming and, therefore, also in exercising extra-territorial jurisdiction on the basis of nationality, but under customary international law, they could have assumed jurisdiction. This does not mean that if England or the United States does not assume this jurisdiction that it may be presumed because it could have done so. This is extremely important because we are talking a lot about international law but, as my colleague Mr. Wladimiroff started with, we are dealing here with a criminal procedure and where the principle of legality is a very important basis to proceed. The next remark I would like to make as far as jurisdiction, I must say jurisdiction under the universality principle, is concerned is the following: The Prosecution has argued that the universal jurisdiction was not an exclusive domestic jurisdiction. To some extent that might be right, but I will try to explain to you why it was never expressed as an exclusive domestic jurisdiction. There never was a need to establish whether this jurisdiction was of an exclusive nature or not because until quite recently, I may say, criminal jurisdiction was exclusively and entirely in the domain of the sovereignty of states. So if we say that it has never been expressed that this was an exclusive jurisdiction, then my answer is there was never a need to do so. Even the precedents of Tokyo and Nuremberg cannot serve for this purpose, because in Tokyo and Nuremberg there was a situation where there was a combined effort of the allied powers to exercise their domestic jurisdiction, which was a combined effort, and then to some extent it becomes national. But the argument has been used by the Defence in the framework of whether national sovereignty was violated by this jurisdiction imposed on the Tribunal, and that was, of course, a totally different situation in Tokyo and Nuremberg where the allied powers combined their efforts and there was no matter of imposing an international jurisdiction of a primary nature. The last remark I would like to make is about the argument that has been made by the Prosecutor on the Nicaragua case that the common Article 3 provisions would be -- I did not hear them say "applicable" -- applicable, but at least they were valid in even a situation of an internal conflict. First of all, I must admit that the decision in the Nicaragua case says that there is a common set of rules that apply. They are not saying the Convention applies, but a common set of rules applies in both international and internal conflicts. But I think we have to clearly understand that this decision has been taken, not in a context of administering criminal law. If you just look at what it would mean, for example, this interpretation, in quite a lot of domestic legislations we will find that in many, many countries in their Statutes, their laws, about war crimes, you will find a reference to the customs of war. If this interpretation would be directly valid, the interpretation by the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case, this would mean, for example, that in quite a lot of countries they would have got, without having asked for it, jurisdiction over all kinds of internal conflicts all over the world which is, clearly, not meant by these states. On the other hand, we also have to look at the consequences under the treaty. I stressed before the importance of the principle of legality in a criminal prosecution. What we are now doing at this moment is, since there is a not very clear provision on jurisdiction in Article 3, we are now trying to interpret and saying, well, because of the decision of the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case, we have to understand that by the jurisdiction granted under Article 3, we also should accept that common Article 3 and the violation of common Article 3 is within the jurisdiction granted in Article 3 of the Statute. I think this again might be a major problem from the point of view of criminal law where I think the basis for jurisdiction should be clear, and it should not be necessary that we have to discuss the matter of what this jurisdiction is because of vague wordings, because of no clear intentions perhaps behind it, and that we have to discuss this in order to find out what exactly is the jurisdiction. I used to work at the university in earlier days. We always said when we were making questions for examinations of students that if we have to discuss the issue more than 10 minutes, it is not clear. I would not say that 10 minutes is good enough, but I think this kind of interpreting and finding sources in order to make the sense of the jurisdiction granted in Article 3 broader might violate the basic principle of legality under criminal law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is there any significance, do you think, in the fact that the Secretary General notes the Nicaragua case in footnote 9 of his report but does so in relation to introducing Article 5 and makes no reference to it in introducing Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I think we have some problem in interpreting the legal history of the Statute, because, as we have found, the Secretary General sometimes takes a different position from voting members of the Security Council. So, in general, that is a problem. But I would say that if he has thought of the Nicaragua case, then it is quite amazing that the common Article 3 is not added to Article 2 of the Statute, and when he raises the issue in relation to Article 5 this would be an argument to make clear that it was not intended that it would be included under Article 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When he includes it in footnote 10, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You are correct -- 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: In my copy, it is nine, funnily.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The reporter is making reference to crimes against humanity. That is for sure. Then he says: "Regardless of whether they are committed in an armed conflict, international or internal in character"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then he cites Nicaragua. Do you believe that then that is support for the proposition that common Article 3 then should be included in Article 3 under our Statute? Is that what you are saying, Mr. Orie? I am sorry, I do not think I am following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No. I am saying that what the Prosecutor defended this morning is that by interpreting Article 3 of the Statute, especially because, apart from summing up some Conventions, there is a remaining part which is not specified, and that on the authority of the decision in the Nicaragua case, that in this remaining part we might include common Article 3 because that is customary international law applicable both on national and international armed conflict and, therefore, it is part of Article 3. What I see from this mentioning by the Secretary General, first of all, is that if he intended to include it, that he intended to include it under Article 5 and not under Article 3, which might be a bit amazing because Article 2 would have been relative, in my opinion, if he had done so, but he uses the authority, I think, in order to explain his position as far as the armed conflicts mentioned in Article 5 has been described as either internal or international. I think that is the main reason why he used this authority in order to try to justify the rather extensive jurisdiction granted in Article 5.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But you say that Article 3 should be limited to, I gather, an international conflict, is that so? I am sorry. Referring to Article 5, although it says international or internal, it is your position that there should be a requirement that it be international. Then he cites Nicaragua in footnote 10, and at least the Prosecutor has told us that that is an indication that there is no international requirement for common Article 3, just internal. I do not understand whether that helps you or hurts you, I guess. I think are you trying to take part of it to help you and then part of it will hurt you, or is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would rather first read again for myself footnote 10 quite precisely. One moment, if you would allow me? As a matter of fact, when I read it quite carefully it might even be worse for the Prosecutor, because it says -- perhaps I will read it aloud -- "In this context it is to be noted that the International Court of Justice has recognised that the prohibitions contained in common Article 3 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions are based on elementary considerations of humanity, and cannot be breached in an armed conflict regardless of whether it is international or internal in character". So, what I read here from the Secretary General, that it cannot be breached at all in an armed conflict which is not understandable to me. I have difficulties in explaining footnote 10, but I did not read it carefully before replying to the question that was put to me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then is your position, how can common Article 3 be included in Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I did respond to the remarks made by the Prosecutor this morning. Because when I did understand him well, he was saying, under Article 5 we meet in armed conflicts, under Article 2 we have the grave breaches. Is a violation of common Article 3, where can it be found in the Articles providing for jurisdiction? If I understood well, they were arguing that it could only be under Article 3 because Article 3, laws and customs of war, included even for an internal conflict the common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. That argument was based upon the Nicaragua case. What we now see is that the Secretary General thinks that they cannot be breached at all which is not quite understandable to me in this context. But I did understand at least his reference to common Article 3 as to explain that common Article 3 would be applicable both in internal and international conflicts. I must say that it is a bit of a puzzle for me to understand what he exactly means, especially because of the word "cannot" or it is a mistake, that is also a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: A misprint.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have a lot of mistakes between the Secretary General and all the authority powers in what they do write down.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin? Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else from the Prosecutor? We will hear a couple and then go back if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will be very quick.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question since we are on this point? Common Article 3, is it your position that common Article 3 is included or at least this Tribunal would have jurisdiction for common Article 3 violations under Article 2 of our Statute and under Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Under Article 3.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Only?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not adopting that novel approach regarding Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not regarding Article 2, no, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But your position is that common Article 3 would be included within Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 3. Now Mr. Orie has said if you look at the footnote of the Secretary General, he says that it would not be applicable in any armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "Cannot" must mean "may not".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It has to be either a typographical error or a mistake of some sort, in our submission. It means you are not allowed to commit an armed conflict regardless of whether it is prohibited.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do not accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do not accept what it says here, "It cannot be breached". We are saying it can be breached in both -- I will just confer with my friend here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I suggest if it said "which cannot be breached", that would make sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That would make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It does not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It does not say that, but it does not make sense as it is now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As I understand it, some members of the Security Council -- well, never mind, I will withdraw that. I will leave that alone. Maybe it was a typo, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just picking up on the matter raised by Mr. Wladimiroff, the issue about the capacity of the Tribunal to review the decisions of the Security Council still seems to be creating some confusion. So I will state it in as succinct a way as I possibly can. In our submission, under the Charter decisions by the Security Council, under Chapter VII, are not reviewable by other organs. However, we must assume that the Security Council could not have intended to violate fundamental human rights principles. Such questions can only be implicated in the Statute and practice of the Tribunal in the interests of justice. Therefore, the Tribunal may review the Statute, the Rules of the Tribunal, but not the decision to create the Tribunal under Chapter VII. In other words, it is our submission that this Tribunal does not have the right of judicial review of decisions of the Security Council, such as you could declare that the actions of the Security Council are null and void and of no effect. It is our submission, your Honours, that you only look to the Statute to satisfy yourselves that a fair trial can be had. Your Honour, I did mention earlier this morning there may have been something in the transcript that troubled us that we wanted to go back to when we had the transcript. I have done that. On page 116 of the transcript there is a reference to an Article by Professor Meron and the Defence referred to the first paragraph as it appears on page 83, I do not want to take your Honours to it. I merely just wish to say if your Honours read on to paragraphs 2 and 3 we submit that you would be better assisted in understanding what Professor Meron was saying at that point. Those are the matters I want to address. I think my friend Mr. Fenrick has a number of matters he wishes to raise briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, my comments will be quite brief. First of all, with reference to the Defence's argument that the Geneva Conventions can be broken up or that we can look at Bosnia from an area-by-area point of view, there is no question whatsoever that the Geneva Conventions apply to states. What we are talking about is the relationship between parties to the Geneva Conventions. Those are states in entirety; not bits and pieces. Secondly, the Defence argued that I could not have my cake and eat it too, and that one could not argue that the Republica of Srpska constitution provided that the people were linked to and still citizens of Yugoslavia, and then go on from there and say that the Republica Srpska has no territory. Yes, I can say that. I have no difficulty saying that whatsoever. What we are saying is that this a group which is physically located in Bosnia, in Bosnian territory, which claims that it has links to Yugoslavia and those claims are embodied in their constitution. Third, it was suggested by the Defence that there is no indication in any of the Prosecution's submissions that the JNA continued to act in Bosnia after 19th May. Yes, there are. Those submissions are contained in document 101 which is the Gow submission and also in our brief itself. The next point has to do also with the grave breach issues. I did say this morning that I regarded the American position on the grave breach provisions applying to common Article 3 as novel and interesting. We do not wish to use that argument as the basis for our submission today. It is possible that at times things which are initially novel and interesting eventually become more useful. It is possible that further analysis might lead us to change our position.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just in case, Mr. Fenrick, you know the book that Mr. Wladimiroff quoted you from -- things can develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, things can develop, your Honour! Next with reference to the supplementary agreements under common Article 3, we have maintained that the October agreement could be used in fact to assist in the interpretation of the 22nd May agreement. I just direct your attention or ask you to pay heed to Article 31 of the Vienna Convention on the law of treaties which does provide that together with the context one can take into account subsequent agreements between the parties and subsequent practice in the application of a treaty in order to determine its precise meaning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is our international contract law?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The Vienna Convention on the law of treaties is basically the contract law. Next the Defence quoted from an Article by Professor Kalshoven. We are not disputing that the Hague Conventions were designed for international armed conflict. In fact they were designed initially for states of declared war. Our argument is that the meaning "laws or customs of war" has a broader meaning now than it did in the past. Before I conclude, there is no question, it is submitted, that the footnote 10 which has been referred to quoting the Nicaragua decision in the Secretary General's report must when it talks about "cannot be breached" means "may not be allowed to be breached". If you take a look at page 51 in our brief there is a detailed quotation from the Nicaragua decision. It is our submission that there is no other conclusion that someone could come to on reading that provision or those parts of the decision. Our last observation is in relation to the argumen on common Article 3 and what might be regarded as creeping universality of jurisdiction, I would just like to bring your attention to a recent Article by Professor Meron "International Criminalisation of Internal Atrocities". On the last page of that Article, page 577, he discusses recent Belgian legislation, the 1993 law, called "Crime de droit Internationale" which provides for criminal jurisdiction of Belgian courts over certain breaches, not only of the Geneva Conventions and Protocol 1 but also of Protocol 2 regardless of the nationality of the victim or perpetrator or where the offence was committed. On the basis of this law, the Brussels Prosecutor's office on 29th May of this year issued several international arrest warrants against persons involved in the atrocities in Rwanda. At least one of those warrants which was issued was issued against a Rwandan responsible for massacres of other Rwandans in Rwanda. In other words, this will not be unprecedented if we move into this field. It is already being done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else for the Prosecution? The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As I indicated, the Chamber has ambitious expectations to render a decision with respect to this motion on jurisdiction on August 10th. We will also be working on the motion for protective measures that the Prosecutor has filed in an attempt to render a decision with respect to that motion as well on August 10th. If there are no other matters we will stand adjourned until August 10th.
